issues.title: About function
issues.author: yangbodong22011
issues.body:
Functions can be invoked at the tail end of a path - the input to a function is the output of the path expression. The function output is dictated by the function itself.

Refer：https://github.com/json-path/JsonPath#functions

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
Thank you for this.  This is one possibility for a syntax for functions.  There are others, e.g. the common syntax `foo(param1, param2, ...)`.

We will need to compare all options before we make a decision.

comments.author: yangbodong22011
comments.body: @gregsdennis Yes, MongoDB operator is also a good choice: https://docs.mongodb.com/manual/reference/operator/query/

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body:
> Functions can be invoked at the tail end of a path - the input to a function is the output of the path expression. The function output is dictated by the function itself.
> 
> Refer：https://github.com/json-path/JsonPath#functions

Many, perhaps most, JSONPath implementations support functions in one form or another, in some cases only in filter expressions, in other cases both in and outside of filter expressions. The former generally restrict JSONPath to selecting elements in the original document only, the latter permit results that are computations performed on the original document.

(1) Implementations that use JavaScript (or Python or PHP) for evaluating JSONPath filter expressions, including original JavaScript Goessner, have access to all the JavaScript (or Python or PHP) functions. For example, they have access to functions that return the Unicode Normalization Form of strings, see [JavaScript String.prototype.normalize](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/normalize) (or [Python unicodedata.normalize](https://docs.python.org/3.6/library/unicodedata.html#unicodedata.normalize) or [PHP normalizer.normalize](https://www.php.net/manual/en/normalizer.normalize.php)).

(2) The important and influential [Jayway implementation](https://github.com/json-path/JsonPath) introduced functions that can be invoked at the tail end of the path, as you mentioned. These can be used to return results that are computations performed on the original document.

(3) A couple of implementations that made up their own filter expression languages support function syntax like
```
$.books[?(tokenize(@.author,'\\s+')[-1] == 'Tolkien')]
```
see e.g. [here](https://danielaparker.github.io/JsonCons.Net/articles/JsonPath/JsonConsJsonPath.html#functions).

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
***NOTE** I definitely think support for functions should **not** be part of the initial release but should be considered for follow-up releases.*

I would like to propose the typical syntax for functions:

```
function_name([param list])
```

- A function name MUST be a string that starts with an alpha char and is followed by any number of alpha-numeric chars and underscores (same character set as `.`-syntax property names).  This should make them easily identifiable in expressions.
- A function MUST have parentheses, even if there are no parameters.
- The parameter list MUST be comma-delimited.  Each parameter may be any valid JSON Path expression, including the constant values that are allowed, e.g. booleans, numbers, etc, but not structured values (unless those are supported by the time functions are implemented).
- A function MUST return a value.

I would also suggest that parameters have an _expected_ type.  If the function receives a value for a parameter that is the wrong type, it should return `false` or some other "negative"-indicating value, much like the existence test.

### Predefined functions to start

#### `length(x)`

Receives any valid JSON Path, probably most commonly `@`, and returns the object or array length of the value at that location.

Optional support:

- non-singular paths - the return value would be the number of results returned by the path.
- string values - the return value would be the string length (probably unicode chars, not byte count)

#### `index()`

Receives no parameters and returns the index / property name of the current item (`@`).  I see no value in attempting to get the key of a specified path.

### Custom function support

Building on this, we could allow for implementations to support user-defined functions, but we'd have to include a statement that user-defined functions would not be expected to be supported the same way or at all in other implementations.

I think this is potentially very powerful as many users use JSON Path simply within their local environment rather than sending paths between systems.

This is something that I would probably support in my implementation (should functions become a syntax) even if it's not supported in the spec.  (Of course, I'd document the interoperability aspects of defining your own functions.)

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body:
> _**NOTE** I definitely think support for functions should **not** be part of the initial release but should be considered for follow-up releases._
> 
Follow up _releases_, in the plural? Wouldn't that negate the primary benefit of an RFC, which is interoperability? 

> Each parameter may be any valid JSON Path expression, including the constant values that are allowed, e.g. booleans, numbers, etc, but not structured values (unless those are supported by the time functions are implemented).

I understand that in the draft it's currently underspecified what JSONPath expressions can evaluate to, but you're not suggesting that they can't evaluate to JSON arrays and objects in any context, are you? Also, if they can evaluate to `undefined`,  as has been proposed, that needs to be part of the type system supported by functions.

> #### `index()`
> Receives no parameters and returns the index / property name of the current item (`@`). 
> 
That doesn't sound like a function, as conventionally understood. Presumably it would need to receive a 'this' or 'self' parameter to access the "current item". Which would also require an extension to the type system needed to support functions.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
> Follow up releases, in the plural?

I don't understand what you're getting at.  I sincerely expect there to be revisions to this document after initial publication.  Why wouldn't there be?  Surely we would want to expand on the feature set.  Otherwise, the spec would never be published.

I worded it that way because I wasn't certain it needed to be the _next_ release.  It could be added into any subsequent release.

> Wouldn't that negate the primary benefit of an RFC, which is interoperability?

How does an RFC imply interoperability?

How does this feature (or multiple versioned releases, maybe?) negate interoperability?  If the spec defines functions, then any implementation of that spec, regardless of language/framework, would also be required to support them as defined.  That's interoperability.

> ... but you're not suggesting that they can't evaluate to JSON arrays and objects in any context, are you?

No, I'm not suggested that.  They can definitely evaluate to arrays and objects.  Any valid value should be able to be passed to a function, but if a function receives a value of a type it's not expecting, it should return a negative result of some kind.  This aligns with the current idea that if a path parses correctly, it should not throw errors upon evaluation.

> if they can evaluate to `undefined`, as has been proposed, that needs to be part of the type system supported by functions.

Yeah.

> That doesn't sound like a function, as conventionally understood.

Why not?  Parameterless functions exist.  I considered using `index(@)`, but then it only makes sense for the parameter to be `@`, so why have it at all?  Not having a parameter means that someone couldn't do `index(@.foo)`, which is a pointless function because it just returns `"foo"`.  Making this a parameterless function makes it hard for users to do things they're not allowed to do or don't make sense.  It already knows that its context is the current item (and the item's parent).  (Presumably, the implementation is iterating through the items in a loop and has access to these things, at which point it can pass that context to whatever implementation it has internally.)

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body:
> > That doesn't sound like a function, as conventionally understood.
> 
> Why not? Parameterless functions exist.

Can you provide an example? I think a parameter-less function must return a constant.

 > I considered using `index(@)`, 

I don't think that works, if you want `index` to be considered a function like any other. In a JSONPath expression, a bare `@` evaluates to a value, a value that does not carry with it any information about the array index or object member name from whence it came. It is only a value. 

Of course, an implementation could use the _notation_ `index(@)` to represent the index or name associated with `@`, but it would be an ad hoc thing, using information unavailable to your custom function, were it to be passed `@`.  

> Making this a parameterless function makes it hard for users to do things they're not allowed to do or don't make sense. It already knows that its context is the current item (and the item's parent).

In order for the function to "know" anything about its context, it needs to be passed a parameter (possibly hidden) such as "this" in C++ or "self" in Python, or otherwise be bound to an environment. To support that would make a specification for functions much more complicated, certainly beyond that of [JMESPath functions](https://jmespath.org/specification.html#built-in-functions), for example.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
Firstly, we're not trying to build a full programming language.  If we were, I might be inclined to agree with you.  But we're trying to build a query syntax, and that affords us some liberties.

I think you're looking at it from a pure-functional point of view.  A pure function would, in most cases, return a constant without any parameters.  But as I said, we're not building a _programming_ language, functional or otherwise.

An example of a parameterless function (in another query language) would be SQL's `DATE()` function, which returns the current date.  It is _defined_ to have the context of the system on which the query is running.  It _never_ returns the same value twice (without adjusting the system or mocking that dependency entirely).

Similarly, the `index()` function could be _defined_ to have the context of the iterator in which it runs, i.e. the filter query `[?()]`.

Since you made a parallel with C++, consider this like a member function that's defined on the iterator itself rather than a static/global function.  Even if you consider `this` as a (hidden) parameter, it doesn't appear as a parameter when you call it ("hidden" 😉);  the parameter list is empty.

`length(x)` acts more like the pure function you're thinking of.  It doesn't need any context; it just acts on the parameter it's given.  But this doesn't mean that `index()` must also work that way.

Lastly, defining `index()` this way opens the door for others functions, and even user-defined functions if we do that, to do similar things, which I think it's extremely useful.  Requiring only pure functions severely inhibits their usefulness.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body:
> Similarly, the index() function could be defined to have the context of the iterator in which it runs, i.e. the filter query [?()].

Okay, I've changed my mind about that, and agree. It's analogous to the XPath `fn:position()` function. I think you'd want separate functions for returning the index for an array and the name for an object member, though.

issues.author: nichtich

**SQL/JSON Path Expression** (as specified in [SQL ISO standard](https://www.iso.org/standard/78937.html)) was heavily inspired by JSONPath, overlaps in both syntax and semantics and has a similar name. issues.title: Make @ optional in filter selectors
issues.author: nichtich
issues.body:
The grammar includes `"@"` only it at `rel-path` rule in filter expressions. `rel-path` is only used in rule `path`:

    path         = rel-path / json-path
    rel-path     = "@" *(S (dot-selector / index-selector))

As `json-path` always starts with `$`, a parser does not need the `"@"` to distinguish between `rel-path` and `json-path`, so the character can be made optional, helping JSONPath expressions look less like obfuscated Per (SCNR).

Example:

    $[? @.key>42 && @.key<44 ]
    $[?  .key>42 &&  .key<44 ]

The latter is more readable, isn't it?

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
We could do this.
Matters of taste aside (I find the version with the @ sign to be more readable), this would be an innovation unless existing implementations already are doing this.
We are not chartered to innovate, except where this is necessary to achieve an interoperable (and evolvable) situation.

comments.author: nichtich
comments.body:
I guess you are accustomed to the `@` so feels natural, but from a usability point of view it is noise and confusing (what's the difference between `@.foo` and `.foo`?  Why is `$.foo` allowed at the root but not `@.foo`?...) *except* when you are already used to it. Making it optional would not break existing JSONPath expressions but it would make existing implementations lack support of a new feature. You decide what weights more: simplicity and usability or keeping existing implementations fully compliant with the spec. As far as I understand, parenthesis in filter expressions (`[?(...)]`) have also been dropped although they were mandatory.

Another argument *against* making `@` optional would be to better align with SQL/JSON Path Expression Syntax.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body:
> what's the difference between `@.foo` and `.foo`? 

I don't know of prior experience with bare expressions that omit only the "current node" symbol, but not the dot. But there is plenty outside of JSONPath for omitting _both_ the "current node" symbol and the dot - see [The "current value" or "current node", and the meaning thereof](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/76). That's the case for JMESPath and XPath. SQL also permits omitting qualifying table names or aliases when there is no ambiguity.

Allowing `foo` in place of `@.foo` does mean that unquoted names should not be allowed to start with a digit, otherwise expressions like `$foo[?(2 == 4)]` would be ambiguous. There is some data about that [here](https://cburgmer.github.io/json-path-comparison/results/filter_expression_with_dot_notation_with_number.html), a minority of JSONPath implementations do allow unquoted names that start with a digit, as did earlier versions of the draft. But it looks like recent versions of the draft do not, so could accommodate your proposal.

> Why is `$.foo` allowed at the root but not `@.foo`?

That's a good question. There was a [proposal by Davide Bettio](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/59) to support `@.foo` at the root, and it was discussed at the [May 2021 ietf meeting](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/minutes-interim-2021-jsonpath-01-202105110900/). The proposal was dismissed with the "consensus" that "Queries should not begin with @, but this is a natural extension point."

It's not obvious from reading the minutes that the committee fully understood that not accomodating JSONPath expressions beginning with `@` was tantamount to asserting that expressions in filters beginning with `@` were not JSONPath expressions (unfortunately Bettio was not present to defend the proposal.) In any case, it's clear in the draft that they are not, the draft defines them as
```
rel-path     = "@" *(S (dot-selector / index-selector))
```

In terms of prior experience, implementations (at least the important ones) group into two categories.

(1) Implementations including original JavaScript Goessner that use JavaScript (or Python or PHP) for evaluating JSONPath filter expressions. In these scripts, `@` is substituted with the "current value", and expressions consisting of the "current value" followed by a dot or a left square bracket are evaluated according to JavaScript (or Python or PHP) rules. This always result in a single value. 

(2) JSONPath implementations that make up their own expression languages.  The important ones (Java Jayway, JSON.Net), regard expressions starting with `@` as JSONPath expressions in their own right, and evaluate them as such. They specify rules for evaluating them as a single value (rather than a list of values) so that evaluations and JSON literals can be meaningfully compared.

The draft authors chose to follow the second group by inventing their own expression language, but the first group by making expressions beginning with `@` somewhat analogous to evaluating JavaScript variables with index and identifier operators. It's unclear to me why they made that choice. I think it would be helpful if they included some notes in the draft to motivate their decisions in terms of prior experience.

issues.title: Specify handing of null
issues.author: glyn
issues.body:
The current spec is silent about how `null` is handled in many situations:

1. What is the result of applying the JSONPath `$` to the JSON document `null`?
2. What is the result of applying the JSONPath `$.*` to the JSON document `{"a": null}`? The [comparison consensus](https://cburgmer.github.io/json-path-comparison/results/dot_notation_on_null_value.html) implies a node set with the single value `null`.
3. What is the result of applying the JSONPath `$[*]` to the JSON document `[null]`? The [comparison consensus](https://cburgmer.github.io/json-path-comparison/results/bracket_notation_with_wildcard_on_null_value_array.html) implies a node set with the single value `null`.
4. What is the result of applying the JSONPath `$[0]` to the JSON document `[null]`? Presumably a node set with the single value `null`.
5. What is the result of applying the JSONPath `$[1:2]` to the JSON document `["a", null, "b"]`? Presumably a node set with the values `"a"` and `null`.
6. What is the result of applying the JSONPath `$[?@]` to the JSON document `["a", null, "b"]`?
7. What is the result of applying the JSONPath `$[?@.a]` to the JSON document `[{"a": null}]`?
8. What is the result of applying the JSONPath `$.null` to the JSON document `{"null": "value"}`? The [comparison consensus](https://cburgmer.github.io/json-path-comparison/results/dot_notation_with_key_named_null.html) implies a node set with the single value `"value"`.

To 7.: https://cburgmer.github.io/json-path-comparison/results/filter_expression_without_value.html

issues.title: Proposal: Value type-checks
issues.author: gregsdennis
issues.body:
***NOTE** I definitely think support for this proposal should **not** be part of the initial release but should be considered for follow-up releases.  I had the idea and wanted to document it.*

## Scenario

Given the following JSON

```json
[
  "foo",
  5,
  { "bar": null },
  "baz",
  null
]
```

there is no way to isolate only string values.

## Proposal

To address this, we should introduce a type check.

I would like to propose the `is` operator for JSON Path expressions in the filter selector `[?()]`.  Examples of usage would be:

```
@ is boolean
@ is string
@ is number
@.foo is object
```

To support this, we would need to reserve `object`, `array`, `boolean`, `number`, `null`, and `string` as reserved keywords in expressions, meaning that functions could not bear these names.  I don't think that this would cause any problems.

It could also support value coercion on the RHS.  For example `@ is $.foo`, could return `true` if `$.foo` is a string containing one of these type keywords.

## A sub-par alternative

I had also considered a `type(x)` function to build on [my proposal for functions](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/160#issuecomment-1069549608).

The `type(x)` function would take a single parameter and return... well that's the problem.  What would it return?  It can't rightly return a string.  It would have to return some implementation-internal concept of a "value type", and then we'd have to add support for equality.

`type(@) == object` and `type(@) == "object"` just don't feel right.

I think the `is` operator is the way to go for this feature.

comments.author: cabo
comments.body: A function syntax would have the advantage that it could use an extension point, while new syntax such as " is " always would lead to harder to manage syntax errors.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
> A function syntax would have the advantage that it could use an extension point, while new syntax such as " is " always would lead to harder to manage syntax errors.


I'm not sure why `is` would be any harder to parse than any other equivalence operator, e.g. `==` or `!=`.

And again, what would a function return?  How would you test that a value is, for example, an array?

issues.title: Descendant semantics
issues.author: bram209
issues.body:
### Dot Wildcard Selector
> A dot-wild-selector acts as a wildcard by selecting the nodes of all member values of an object in its input nodelist as well as all element nodes of an array in its input nodelist.

Considering the following input:
```json
{
  "o": {"j": 1, "k": 2},
  "a": [5, 3]
}
```

`$.*` would evaluate to (in this case the values of the object):

```json
[
  {"j": 1, "k": 2},
  [5, 3]
]
```

### Descendant Selector

I would expect the descendant version: `$..*` to evaluate to:
```json
[
  {"j": 1, "k": 2},
  [5, 3],
  1,
  2,
  5,
  3
]
```

Yet the example says:
```json
[
  { "o": {"j": 1, "k": 2}, "a": [5, 3] }, // full input is selected, even tho the dot wildcard selector would only select the object values
  {"j": 1, "k": 2},
  [5, 3],
  1,
  2,
  5,
  3
]
```
Considering the following pseudo logic:
```
function traverse(json_value, child_selector) {
     if (json_value == array) {
          return child_selector.select(json_value) + json_value.map(x => traverse(x, child_selector));
    } else if (json_value == object) {
          return child_selector.select(json_value) + json_value.values.map(x => traverse(x, child_selector));
   } else {
         return [];
   }
}
```

In the case of `$..*` the `child_selector` would be an index wildcard selector.

### Expected Descendant semantics
I would expect the descendant selector to (starting by selecting itself) walk through the json structure and select all the results by applying the child selector (dot-member-name, index-selector, index-wild-selector, or wildcard) on each traversed value.

Am I misunderstanding something here or is this the intended behavior?

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
Thanks for raising this. When I was writing the example, I noticed that only a few implementations included the node itself. But the descendant selector semantics currently say:
> The descendant-selector selects the node and all its descendants.

and so I included the "starting" node itself. This is why I included the following text in the commit message:

> [Note] that contrary to the consensus of the comparison project (below), the root node appears in the results of $..* and $..[*].
> 
>    https://cburgmer.github.io/json-path-comparison/results/dot_notation_with_wildcard_after_recursive_descent.html

The semantics section needs improving anyway to clarify the semantics of the various forms of the descendants selector. I agree with the semantics proposed above, providing there is a consensus for this in the WG.

comments.author: goessner
comments.body:
In my understanding descendant selector `$..*` simply extends the single-level operating of child selector `$.*` , in that it further recursively operates on all other descendant levels.

So I agree to Bram's traversal algorithm above.

A node is not considered a descendant of itself. Obviously I have not been aware of this behavior.

issues.title: Filter expressions: confusing 'exists' semantics
issues.author: bram209
issues.body:
Considering that, according to the grammar, `exist-expr` is a `boolean-exrp`:

```
exist-expr        = [neg-op S] singular-path 
```

And the following note:
> A member or element value by itself in a Boolean context is interpreted as false only if it does not exist. Otherwise it is interpreted as true. To be more specific about the actual value, explicit comparisons are necessary. This existence test -- as an exception to the general rule -- also works with structured values.

So this would mean that a singular path that points to a boolean `false` value would evaluate to `true`.

```json
[
   { "id": 1, "isActive": true },
   { "id": 2, "isActive": false },
   { "id": 3, "isActive": true },
]
```
People might try:
`$[?(@.isActive)]` to get the active elements but will be surprised to see all elements returned.

I think this kind of query is quite common and for people with a developer background it would feel unnatural to type `boolean expression == true`

On the other side,  the need for queries that check *implicitly* for existence feels rarer to me (from my experience mostly well-typed tagged unions are used to structure JSON), which makes me wonder if `exists` should be a function instead (once functions get added to the spec).

This would make the `exists` check more explicit and therefore less confusing, in my opinion.

### Proposed solution
Personally, I would like to:
- have an explicit way of checking existence.
- evaluate singular path to a boolean value (which could be seen as a tautological statement) in the above example

When a singular path is given as a boolean expression but does not point to a boolean value, it gets a bit tricky:
- it could throw an error at the evaluation
- evaluate to false always
- introduce the concept of truthy & falsy values, which could serve similar use cases as `exists`, in this case, `true` would be `truthy` and `false` would be falsy and the above described problem would go away

I normally am more a statically typed programming language guy so not too keen on the concept of truthy & falsy values, but considering this is a query language for JSON, it might make more sense...


Thoughts?

comments.author: bram209
comments.body:
another possibility (that does not rely on functions) is to introduce a new primitive value `undefined` so one would type:
`$[?(@.prop != undefined)]`

comments.author: glyn
comments.body: Unfortunately, there isn't much of a consensus among implementations: [comparison project example](https://cburgmer.github.io/json-path-comparison/results/filter_expression_with_value.html).

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
In a statically typed language with a Boolean-typed variable `x`,

```
if x == true {...}
```

definitely is a code smell, usually outing a complete noob.

But this isn't a statically typed language with a Boolean type.
(JSON is schema-free and thus dynamically typed, and there is nothing that even justifies the introduction of RFC 8259 to mention "booleans" (sic); the [actual definition](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259#section-3) only knows the three separate and independent values false, null, and true.)

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
> JSON is schema-free and thus dynamically typed

This is just wrong.  _Javascript_ is dynamically typed because it considers objects with different property sets to be different types.  _JSON_ is statically typed: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, and the constants `true`, `false`, and `null`.  (Practically speaking, `true` and `false` are booleans.  Making this distinction is splitting hairs and not worth our time.)  For JSON, objects with different property sets, while they are not equivalent, are still the same type: `object`.

> introduce a new primitive value `undefined`...

We've had plenty of conversations stating that we don't want to introduce `undefined` as a value.  To reiterate the above, JSON isn't Javascript; there is no `undefined` in JSON.

> `if x == true {...}` definitely is a code smell

Agreed, but the point of the argument is that for the expression `!x`, `x` _appears_ to represent some boolean-ish value, and then the `!` operator is negating that result.

We also have declared that expressions in filter selectors (`[?(<expr>)]`) must return boolean values.

This results in a syntactical ambiguity for `[?(!@.foo)]`:

- Is the user testing for the existence of a property?
- Is the user testing for the "truthiness" of the value at that property?

The _only_ way to know for sure is by forcing `!` followed by a local path (e.g. `!@.foo`) to mean an existence test, which means the _only_ way to check for "truthiness" is to compare with a `true` or `false` constant.

For what it's worth, my implementation, https://json-everything.net/json-path, returns all three items for the example above, acting as a true existence test.  This means that for my library, you MUST use `x == true` to only get the "truthy" ones.

---

To summarize, I see two options to resolve this ambiguity:

1. An expression in the form `!@.foo` is defined explicitly as an existence test, which forces path authors to use expressions like `x == true` for "truthiness" checks (`!@.foo` would return three items from the above example).
2. Expressions strictly return booleans except in the special case of `!@.foo`, for which the expression is "truthy" or "falsy."  This forces some other form of existence test, e.g. a function form like `exists(@.foo)` (`!@.foo` would return two items from the above example).

***NOTE** We've also discussed truthiness at length, and if I recall, we decided against it.  I use it here solely to illustrate my point.*

comments.author: glyn
comments.body: The current specification seems sufficient. Closing.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
My issue isn't that existing paths can be handled by new implementations (what we're calling "backward comparability"), but rather the inverse: new paths won't be handled by existing implementations ("forward compatibility").

Users _will_ complain that their paths, which don't have parentheses, don't work.  Implementors will respond with, "You need parentheses," and then users will be trained to use parentheses anyway.

As it stands, most users are _already_ trained to use parentheses because existing implementations require them.

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
> My issue isn't that existing paths can be handled by new implementations (what we're calling "backward compatibility"), but rather the inverse: new paths won't be handled by existing implementations ("forward compatibility").

Right.  For new features we can't expect forward compatibility anyway.  The discussion here was whether it is worth to reduce forward compatibility by admitting new syntax for existing, widely implemented features.  And I grudgingly have to acknowledge that that is a different question.

> Users _will_ complain that their paths, which don't have parentheses, don't work. Implementors will respond with, "You need parentheses," and then users will be trained to use parentheses anyway.

Actually, implementers will quickly fix that.
Between competing implementations, there is a race to accept the largest amount of inputs (within reason, i.e., balancing it with the cost of implementing them).

But, yes, query creators that care about widest compatibility will be trained to use the parentheses.

(For me, actually, having a feature that only new implementations can understand is a feature.  So the expression will break on implementations that haven't been updated.  Darwin.  And a nice canary.)

> As it stands, most users are _already_ trained to use parentheses because existing implementations require them.

Yes, which is part of the reason why I still think we would better give up on forward compatibility here in favor of cleaning up the query language.  But that is now a matter of taste, and I have to accept that there is a valid argument to the contrary.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body:
> My issue isn't that existing paths can be handled by new implementations (what we're calling "backward comparability"), but rather the inverse: new paths won't be handled by existing implementations ("forward compatibility").

Are you only concerned with new syntax? What about new semantics? For example, the draft is proposing new order of precedence rules that are different from all implementations and languages that I know of, including those of Python, JavaScript and C that some other implementations are following, so there are bound to be expressions that are syntactically the same but would now give the "wrong" result in existing implementations.   

I just don't think it makes sense to go down this road. Users will understand that IETF JsonPath is just another take on the idea of JSONPath, an idea that took major forks from very early on. Any Stack Overflow question on JSONPath quickly establishes that the answers are generally implementation specific.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
I'm going to stop pushing this, but I would like to add this last comment.

JSON Schema has had several forward-incompatible changes over the years as well that I've been fine with.  But the difference between this and those is that JSON Schema is already published and versioned.  It's easy to tell people, "As of version _X_, this feature works differently."

We're not technically versioned as yet because we don't really have a proper publication from which a full implementation can be built (because we're not done).  It feels different to make this change for a 1.0.

But I'll follow the team's consensus.

issues.title: Security considerations first para unconvincing
issues.author: timbray
issues.body:
I'm having trouble understanding or believing the first paragraph of Section 5.1, Attack vectors on JSONPath Implementations.  It's saying, essentially, "Everyone knows that you should never call eval() when processing JSON, so don't do that".  I have two difficulties:

1. JSONpaths aren't in JSON. I can't imagine anyone feeding `$.a[?@>3.5]` to an evaluator.  So I'm not sure the advice adds value.  And if I wanted to use a parser generator to build my parser based on the ABNF in the RFC, what's the harm in that?
2. The data you're applying the JSONpath to *is* in JSON.  I don't think there's any harm in using your programming language's equivalent of JSON.parse() to that as part of evaluating the JSONpath, and this paragraph might scare people away from doing that.

I think it would better just to lose this paragraph.

No, but that doesn’t change the fact that historically people have fed extractions of JSONPath expressions to a PHP or JS engine.
(The paragraph does start with “historically”.)

The @>3.5 after an s/@/a literal for the current value/g very much so.

It could be shortened to “don’t put unvalidated extractions from a JSONPath expression deep into unprotected bowels of your dynamic language interpreter”.

> And if I wanted to use a parser generator to build my parser based on the ABNF in the RFC, what's the harm in that?

Absolutely no harm with that; that’s what the paragraph essentially recommends.

> 	• The data you're applying the JSONpath to is in JSON. I don't think there's any harm in using your programming language's equivalent of JSON.parse() to that as part of evaluating the JSONpath,

No.  Just don’t feed it directly to your interpreter.

How?

Grüße, Carsten

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
> historically people have fed extractions of JSONPath expressions to a PHP or JS engine

I think if people do this, anything that happens as a result is their own fault.  "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes."

I can understand why people think they _can_ do it: the original blog post says that expressions use the syntax of the underlying language.  But in the interest of interoperability, we're not doing that.  I don't think that this practice will hold with our custom expression language.  It may work with _some_ languages, but it'll be purely coincidental, like how I could write JS code that would technically compile under C#.

TBH, I don't know that it's our responsibility to express security concerns, except maybe to warn implementers to protect against malicious usages.  They certainly shouldn't be in the specification  If you want, we can maintain a separate (published, but unofficial) list of known attack vectors and ways implementers can mitigate them.  However, trying to conceive of ways that JSON Path can be exploited so that they can be listed in the specification will lead us down a rabbit hole.  Secondly, if a new vector is found, do we release a new version of the specification?  This isn't scalable.

issues.title: Security Considerations 2nd section upgrade
issues.author: timbray
issues.body:
I have read the latest draft of section 5.2 "Attacks on Security Mechanisms that Employ JSONPath" and I'm having trouble figuring out what it's saying and what would be useful for implementors.

On consideration, I think the following is true.  If the JSON text to which you're applying a JSONpath follows the rules of I-JSON [RFC7493] the results should be deterministic and repeatable for the same JSON text from one JSONpath implementation to another. On the other hand, if you have JSON with dupe object keys, or 300-digit numbers, or broken UTF16 surrogates, you really have no expectation of deterministic behavior.   I *think* (do others agree?) that given I-JSON, conforming JSONpath implementations should be deterministic?

Anyhow, I'd replace section 5.2 with text saying something like "If your security mechanism includes the use of JSONpath implementations, you should be aware that results will be nondeterministic and interoperation can fail if a JSON text you are processing includes constructs that are deprecated but allowed by [RFC8259]. Deterministic behavior can be expected for any JSON text conformant with [RFC7493].

comments.author: glyn
comments.body: Note that in https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/196, I didn't adopt the language above to describe certain constructs as "deprecated but allowed" by RFC 8259 since that RFC does not use the term deprecation. Please feel free to object to this in the PR.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body: It's been previously mentioned in the issues, but the draft should say something about the danger of attack from a query that triggers overflow in a recursive step. The JSONPath recursion operator, given how it's implemented in many implementations, is vulnerable to attack, in situations where a JSONPath expression is provided as a parameter. It's pretty obvious that some, perhaps even most, implementations would not be able to pass Google fuzzer, were that a scenario. Note that enterprises take the risk of vulnerability through recursion very seriously.  In my opinion, some limits on recursion levels ought to be specified.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
Interesting. Wouldn't such a stack overflow attack be bounded by the JSON document? I guess where an attacker can provide _both_ the JSON document and the JSONPath, there is an opportunity for stack overflow. But there is a more general resource exhaustion attack if attackers are allowed to provide arbitrarily large JSON documents.

I agree that JSONPath implementations may wish to defend themselves by imposing recusion limits, memory limits, etc., but I'm not sure I'd want to go as far as requiring specific limits in the spec.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body:
> Interesting. Wouldn't such a stack overflow attack be bounded by the JSON document?

I believe so, but as you also mention, the attacker could supply both. Or supply a document that exploits a JSONPath with a recursive operator.

Of course, a hostile document raises more issues than for just JSONPath. Pull parsers also may exhibit recursion, Microsoft guards against that by limiting .Net JSON parser depth by default to 64. 

My own view is that in today's world, anything that suggests recursion should be flagged.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body: Ok, and based on the advice in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3552 on DOS attacks, I'll put together a PR to flag up the risk of a DOS attack due to recursion and see how that goes down.

issues.title: Operator Precedence
issues.author: danielaparker
issues.body:
## Draft Operator Precedence

The proposed operator precedence in the draft is shown below.

Precedence | Operator type | Syntax
-- | -- | --
5 | Grouping | (...)
4 | Logical NOT | !
3 | Relations | ==, !=,<, <=, >, >=,=~
2 | Logical AND | &&
1 | Logical OR | \|\|

It is assumed that these precedences are motivated by existing languages, but it is also noted that operator precedence is different in different languages such as JavaScript and Python. For example, logical not has low precedence in Python but high precedence in JavaScript and C. The less than/greater than operators have higher precedence than the equality operators in JavaScript and C, but the same precedence in Python. Existing JSONPath implementations that follow these languages for evaluating filter expressions will also have these differences. 

This issue, created by request, collects the comparable operator precedences for Python, JavaScript, Perl, C And XPath 3.1, to illustrate where they're similar to the draft, and where they differ. Perl is included because of these languages, it is the only one that has a `=~` operator. Note that in Perl, the precedence of the `=~` operator is higher than the comparison operators. 

One comment: the draft operator precedence table should include an additional column for associativity, which is needed to fully describe the operator. The unary logical not operator should be shown as "right associative", and the binary operators should be shown as "left associative". 

## JavaScript Operator Precedence

Precedence | Operator type | Syntax|Associativity
-- | -- | --|--
7| Parentheses (grouping)|(...)|n/a
6| Member Access, Computed Member Access|. a[]|left to right
5| Logical NOT|! …|right to left
4|Less Than,Less Than Or Equal,Greater Than,Greater Than Or Equal,in|< <= > >= in|left to right
3|Equality,Inequality|== !=|left to right
2|Logical AND|&&|left to right
1|Logical OR||||left to right

Source: [JavaScript Operator Precedence](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Operator_Precedence#table)

## Perl Operator Precedence

Precedence | Operator type | Syntax|Associativity
-- | -- | --|--
9|Not (high precedence version)|!|left
8|Regex match|=~ |left
7|Comparison|< > <= >= lt gt le ge|chained 
6|Equal,not equal|== != |chain na
5|Logical and|&&|left
4|Logical or||||left
3|Not (low precedence version)|not|right
2|Logical and (lower precedence version)|and|left
1|Logical or (higher precedence version)|or|left 

Source: [Perl Operator Precedence](https://perldoc.perl.org/5.005/perlop#SYNOPSIS)

Remarks:

- Unary "not" is equivalent to "!" except for lower precedence.
- Binary "and" and "or" are equivalent to && and || except lower precedence

## C Operator Precedence

Precedence | Operator type | Syntax|Associativity
-- | -- | --|--
6|Subscript, member access|a[] .|Left to right
5|Logical not|!|Right to left
4|Relational operators|<   <=   >   >=|Left to right
3|Equality operators|== !=|Left to right
2|Logical and|&&|Left to right
1|Logical or||||Left to right

Source: [C Operator Precedence](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/operator_precedence)

## Python Operator Precedence

Precedence | Operator type | Syntax
-- | -- | --
8| Parentheses (grouping)|()
7|Slicing|x[index:index]
6|Subscription|x[index]
5|Attribute reference|x.attribute
4|Comparisons, membership, identity|in, not in, is, is not, <, <=,  >,  >=,<>, !=, ==
3|Boolean NOT|not x
2|Boolean AND|and
1|Boolean OR|or

Source: [Python Operator Precedence](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#operator-precedence)

## XPath 3.1 Operator Precedence

Precedence | Operator type | Syntax|Associativity
-- | -- | --|--
3|Comparisons|eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge, =, !=, <, <=, >, >=|NA
2|Logical and|and|Either	
1|Logical or|or|Either	

Source: [XPath 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-31/#id-precedence-order)

Remarks:

- XPath 3.1 and XQuery don't have a logical not operator, there's a `!` operator, but it's a binary operator that means something different. Instead, XPath 3.1 and XQuery provide the function [fn:not](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-functions-31/#func-not), whose precedence rules follow the rules for functions.

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
Let me try to summarize the objectives here:

* The extension mechanism specifies the grammar for all jsonpath queries that make use of this mechanism, i.e., the individual extensions do not define additional grammar
* A consumer of queries can there parse any extended query; this allows it to find out which extensions are being used in a query (as a list of names)
* We include one feature in jsonpath-base that makes use of the extension mechanism (so far, a length feature has had the most support)
* Extensions are defined in an IANA registry that would initially be populated with the one extension we include
* The registration policy (RFC 8126) for that registry needs to be decided, probably on the spectrum between Specification Required (with some specific instructions to the designated expert) and IETF review.

issues.title: Remove periods at the ends of the selector descriptions
issues.author: gregsdennis
issues.body:
[Section 3.5](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base#section-3.5) contains a bulleted list of the selector types.  Each of the items in the list ends with a period.  While it may (or may not) be grammatically correct, it leads to some confusing text, specifically when a selector contains, or completely comprises of, periods.

For example:

```
 *  Descendants selector ...
```

Because we only have plain text, it's really difficult to see what's going on here.  Formatted, it would look like

> - Descendants selector `..`.

which is much clearer.

If the spec is to continue being issued in a plain text format, I suggest we remove the ending periods from these lines.

issues.title: Syntax breakdown model for selectors needs to be reworked
issues.author: gregsdennis
issues.body:
I think we've cornered ourselves with the way we've defined the selectors, specifically around the array-format selectors.

Implementing a parser for JSON Path, it feels more correct to say that the bracket syntax houses (potentially) multiple selectors.

In [Section 3.5](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base#section-3.5), The text gives examples of thes selectors by including the brackets:

```
   *  Index selector [<index>], where <index> is either a (possibly negative, see Section "Semantics") array index or an object member name.
   *  Index wildcard selector [*].
   *  Array slice selector [<start>:<end>:<step>], where the optional values <start>, <end>, and <step> are integer literals.
   *  Descendants selector ...
   *  List selector [<sel1>,<sel2>,...,<selN>], holding a comma separated list of index and slice selectors.
   *  Filter selector [?(<expr>)]
```

If instead we describe each select without the brackets, and describe the brackets as merely a housing for one or more selectors, then we can actually remove the "list" selector as it becomes defined implicitly.  I would change the above to

```
   *  Name selector '<name>', where <name> is a string key of an object.
   *  Index selector <index>, where <index> is either a (possibly negative, see Section "Semantics") array index.
   *  Index wildcard selector *.
   *  Array slice selector <start>:<end>:<step>, where the optional values <start>, <end>, and <step> are integer literals.
   *  Descendants selector ...
   *  Filter selector ?(<expr>)
```

along with some text stating that each of these must be contained within brackets and may be combined by comma-delimiting them within the brackets.

***NOTE**  In the above, I've removed List Selector and added Name Selector (split from Index).*

From an implementor's point of view, this makes a lot more sense.

The spec isn't written in stone.  We can still change and improve it.  To say this is throwing your hands up in defeat and saying, "Well, it's this way now.  I guess that's it."

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
I'd like to explain an interesting nuance around defining the descendant selector as just `..`.

`..` recursively selects all children separately from the selector that follows it _before_ the next selector runs.  It may appear that the next selector would lose the structural information it needs, but it doesn't because _all_ values are selected, including the intermediate ones.

For example

```json
{
  "foo": [
    1, 
    2, 
    {
      "bar": [ 
        3, 
        4 
      ]
    } 
  ] 
}
```

```jsonpath
$..[1]
```

As a control, the current document says we should expect the output to be a nodelist containing `2` and `4`.

Breaking down the proposal, we get

| selector | nodelist |
|:---|:---|
| `$` | `{"foo":[1,2,{"bar":[3,4]}]}` |
| `..` | `{"foo":[1,2,{"bar":[3,4]}]}`, `[1,2,{"bar":[3,4]}]`, `1`, `2`, `{"bar":[3,4]}`, `[3,4]`, `3`, `4` |
| `[1]` | `2`, `4` |

(`[1]` only acts on the arrays `[1,2,{"bar":[3,4]}]` and `[3,4]`.)

So the result is the same.

I think that implementations could (if they so choose) optimize by processing `..` and the following selector together, but putting `..` in the spec as its own selector makes a clearer breakdown of the syntax and what it's actually doing.  I believe such optimization (e.g. defining `..[1]` as a selector) is a choice of the implementation, not something that should be in the spec.

comments.author: goessner
comments.body:
@gregsdennis: hmm ... to a certain extent I agree to be able to sharpen the semantics of selectors somewhat.

In my mind model we can atomize selectors into *accessors* and *indexes*.

| accessor | allows ... |
|:---:|:---|
| `.` | accessing members of objects |
| `[]` | accessing children of structured values |
| `..` | accessing descendents of structured values |

There is also a composite accessor `..[]`, which is still an accessor. Apart from this exception, accessors cannot be combined.

* *accessors* are not *selectors*.
* *accessors* need to be combined with *indexes* to become *selectors*.
* selectors can be chained.

This way a discussion, what to do with triple dot `...` is obsolete. Especially accessor `..` is no selector on its own. This conforms to current draft.

Then we can identify indexes (also called *clause* recently, which I think is not necessary to introduce as a new term):

| index |  |
|:---:|:---|
| `*` | wildcard index |
| `'name'` | object member index |
| `<int>` | array element index |
| `<start>:<end>:<step>` | array slice index |
| `?...` | filter index |
| `...,...` | list index |

There are constraints with combining accessors and indexes. The most restrictive are `.` and `..`, where only object member index without quotation marks and wildcard index are allowed. The least restrictive are `[]` and `..[]`.

Because of these documentation intensive constraints, I think that the current draft gets it pretty right, to focus on documenting selectors.

But if it is of some help for users and implementers, we can add some atomizing semantics (syntax?) in the draft.

There are two selectors, that cannot be atomized. `$` and `@`.

| JSONPath          | Description                                                                                                           |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| `[*]`             | [wildcard selector](#index-wildcard-selector): selects all immediate descendants of objects and arrays                |
| `..[*]`           | [descendant wildcard selector](#descendant-selectors): recursive version of the wildcard selector                     |
| `[<criteria>]`    | [value selector](#value-selector) for JSON objects and arrays; contains one or more clauses, separated by commas      |
| `..[<criteria>]`  | [descendant value selector](#descendant-selectors) recursive version of the value selector                            |
| `'name'`          | [name criterion](#index-criterion): index current node as an object                                                   |
| `3`               | [index criterion](#index-criterion): index current node as an array (from 0)                                          |
| `0:100:5`         | [array slice criterion](#slice): start:end:step for arrays                                                            |
| `?...`            | [filter criterion](#filter-criterion): selection based on expressions by applying the expression to each child node   |
| `@`               | [current node selector](#filter-criterion) (valid only within filter clauses)                                         |
| `.name`           | shorthand for `['name']`                                                                                              |
| `.*`              | shorthand for `.*`                                                                                                    |
| `..name`          | shorthand for `..['name']`                                                                                            |
| `..*`             | shorthand for `..[*]`                                                                                                 |

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
I think we could be doing this in a more structured fashion.

When setting up terminology, you have two distinct steps:

1. Identifying the categories that will be named.  This is based on the way the categories differ; a sharp delineation is desired, and the categories of course need to be useful.

2. Naming the categories.  This only happens after the categories are well-defined.  Of course, when writing a paper, you never reveal this process, but it is very important not to use preliminary names that may mean different things to different participants of the discussion.

Contrary to other parts of the design process, there is surprisingly little feedback from step 2 to step 1 -- rarely does the naming step reveal information about a category that informs going back to design decisions of step 1.

To facilitate discussion, categories may receive preliminary names in step 1.
Preliminary names better are not names that have been used before, as these have the diverse connotations for different people.  I'll solve that problem here by prefixing my step 1 names with an asterisk.

So let me try to outline step 1.

We need to name certain parts of a query.

1. The part that starts a query.  Currently `$` or `@`. `*starter`.
2. The part that can be appended to a query to form another query. `*appender`.

`*appenders` come in two categories:

2a. `*canonical *appenders`, forms that include a pair of brackets, which carry a comma separated list of `*pickers`.
2b. forms that are `*shortcuts` for some subset of (2a), i.e., each `*shortcut` has a single well-defined equivalent `*canonical *appender`.

I think we have 2b nailed down nicely, so let's look at 2a and their `*pickers`.

The current semantics makes a difference beween how wildcard `*pickers` can be combined and how non-wildcard ones can.  This is probably best fixed, provided that we can properly define the semantics of mixed-`*picker` `*canonical *appenders`.  We need to do that.  I'll assume here all `*pickers` are freely combinable; this is in the interest of both ease of implementation and to keep the specification more concise.

Note that the above alludes to purely syntactical form only in the distinction between 2a and 2b, which is indeed syntactical in nature and can therefore be ignored when defining the semantics.

Only two `*canonical *appenders` remain.  One lets the `*pickers` operate on the children tier only, the other one lets them operate on all descendants.
It may be possible (and certainly is highly desirable) to define the interface between `*appender` and its `*pickers` used inside in a way that `*appenders` and `*pickers` remain orthogonal.  We need to do that.  (We need to properly define the output sequence implications anyway.)

| `<start>:<end>:<step>` | array slice index |
| `?...` | filter |

*pickers are orthogonal to the last two *appenders, as they are freely combinable.
I need to get used to that orthogonality. I am familiar with `orthogonal = perpendicular` in a more geometrical sense. But I can easily approaching that here by thinking of two independent coordinate axes.

Yeah, except that I'm really more interested in the *canonical ones; the *shortcuts are just syntactic sugar.

issues.title: Add extension point
issues.author: cabo
issues.body:
At the June interim, we discussed extension points, and decided we should have one.
This issue is intended to hold discussion of the extension point until we have a complete proposal.

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
This proposal will be informed by the discussion in #160.

The general idea is to have a function-calling-style syntax with a comma-separated argument list in parentheses following a name:

```
function-call = id S "(" S [ arg *( S "," S arg)] ")"
```

id is the typical `[-a-z][-a-z0-9]*`, where we can discuss whether this should indeed be pure kebab, and indeed be lower-case only (both of which would be my strong preference).

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
The names of the id (function-name) go into a registry, which probably should be on the spectrum between specification-required and IETF review, which we'll need to discuss.

The base spec comes with one such preregistered function, `length`, the exact semantics need to be defined (separate issue, e.g., what is its domain, what does it count, ...).  The idea is to make sure people do implement the extension point mechanism and don't just ignore it (See RFC 9170).

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
Two items are less clear:

* What is `arg`?
* Where does the `function-call` production go into?

We have split the expression language into boolean expressions and comparable; these two don't mix except through a comparison.  Comparables have a subset of JSON types available to them, boolean expressions obviously not.  What a path (currently always singular-path) is evaluated to depends on the place in that structure it is used in: In a comparable, if extracts the JSON value a path points to (which is why it needs to be singular there), in a boolean expression it checks existence (is there at least one node matching this path ➔ true, false otherwise).

So what does `flobble(@.foo)` mean?
(Of course, we could leave that interpretation to specific functions, essentially giving formal parameters a type of json-value vs. boolean.  People could force boolean evaluation using `!!@.foo`.)

Where does the function go?  It could go into the the two places where a singular-path can go right now.  We'd have a similar type issue there.

(I'm not sure we need more fine-grained type checking here, but we do need to define what a path means.)

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
> id is the typical `[-a-z][-a-z0-9]*`

Am I reading this right that it includes hyphen `-`?  Was that meant to be underscore `_`?  We've already decided that hyphen wasn't allowed in property names (in dot-syntax).  They should probably be the same.

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
> Am I reading this right that it includes hyphen `-`?

That would be my standard proposal.  But maybe we should keep the path open to eventually embracing arithmetic, which would use U+002D HYPHEN-MINUS for subtraction.  So this should be `[_a-z][_a-z0-9]*`.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
Related to #194 (maybe duplicate)
Also related to #154

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
As pointed out in https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/209#issuecomment-1167664526:

> [if functions are supported, the spec will need to specify] what it means for an expression that evaluates to "absent" to be passed to a function

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body: If "absent" is taken to mean an empty "node set" it may be worth comparing with how [XPath and XQuery Functions and Operators 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-functions-31/) look at an "empty sequence" as an argument to a function. In the XPath/XQuery model, functions have metadata that describe what parameter types they accept, anything else is considered an error. Translating this to JSON, the parameter types would be the usual `null`, `true`, `false`, `number`, `string`, `object`, `array`. These types could be annotated to indicate that either a value of that type or the "empty sequence" is allowed. This corresponds roughly to the idea of "nullable types" in C# or `std::optional` in C++.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body: Or function parameters could all be node lists, and a JSON value is coerced to a node list containing only that value (like an implicit type cast).

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body: @gregsdennis,think about what your function interfaces would look like if you took that approach, it would be awkward compared to the XPath approach. The only information that an empty node list (empty sequence) conveys is non-existence, which in actual implementations can be represented by `undefined` in Javascript, an undefined `JSONValueKind` in a C# `JsonElement` value, an empty `Optional` instance in Java, and so on.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
But doing it by passing a node list means we can use the empty list to represent `undefined` (or whatever you want to call it) with having to explicitly define `undefined`, which is something that we're already trying to avoid.

`length(@)` is literally passing a node list containing the current value because `@` represents a path which returns a node list containing just the current node.  Similarly for `length(@.foo)`.

It follows then that something like `length('string')`, would implicitly wrap `'string'` in a node list. (Passing explicit values may be useful for other potential functions, e.g. `min(@, 10)`.)

Introducing `undefined` as a value is a suggestion that has been repeatedly turned down by the WG.  Let's please close the lid on that one.  This approach shows that we don't need it.

---

One thing we _do_ need to define, however, is return value.  For strings, it makes sense to return the number of characters (or maybe Unicode code points?).  For arrays or objects, it could return the count of members.

What would it do for numbers or the JSON constants `null`, `true`, and `false`?

In C#, queries for the index of an item on arrays return -1 to indicate that the item does not exist in the array.  This world because the index is supposed to be a non-negative valid, so -1 is an expected error state (an error that doesn't warrant throwing an exception). We could do something similar, but I'm not sure how useful that would be.

comments.author: danielaparker
cabo
comments.body:
So at the extension point level, we would probably support both nodelists and JSON values, both as arguments/parameters and as return values.
For a length function, the return value if the argument it is called with does not have a length, probably should fit into the general mold that comparisons return false outside the domain of the comparison operator.  This seems to argue for returning false.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body: Is the committee thinking about supporting functions as an argument to functions, like [jsonata](https://docs.jsonata.org/higher-order-functions) and [XPath 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-functions-31/#datatypes)? JMESPath doesn't, but does support ["expression types"](https://jmespath.org/specification.html#functions), which are similar to lambdas or anonymous functions.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body: I think that's a bit of an advanced use case and can be added after we have initial function support in.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
> Is the committee thinking about supporting functions as an argument to functions, like [jsonata](https://docs.jsonata.org/higher-order-functions) and [XPath 3.1](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-functions-31/#datatypes)? JMESPath doesn't, but does support ["expression types"](https://jmespath.org/specification.html#functions), which are similar to lambdas or anonymous functions.

I was just thinking about this the other day and my position is that the extra cost in the spec (and therefore on implementers and, in terms of cognitive load, on users) is considerably more than the likely benefit. So I think we should at least defer this beyond v1 and possibly indefinitely.

comments.author: cabo
comments.body: Function parameters will become useful if functions can be defined by the query creator.  We are quite a bit away from this level of generality, so I don't think we need to address this.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body: A function extension point was added in base 09.

issues.title: Move filter semantics out of syntax section
issues.author: glyn
issues.body: Currently the syntax section of the "Filter Selector" section describes some semantics. These descriptions should be folded into the semantics section.

issues.title: absent >= absent?
issues.author: glyn
issues.body:
(This is a follow-on from https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/123)

https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/207 covers comparing absent with absent using == and !=, but we still haven't decided what to do about the likes of "absent >= absent". The spec currently says:

> Comparisons using one of the operators <, <=, >, and >= are between numeric values only. Using these operators to compare other types of values produces a "false" comparison result.

This doesn't make it clear what to do when comparing two singular paths which each select no value.

I can see two options:

1. We might want "absent >= absent" to be true because "absent == absent" is true.

2. We might say that "absent" isn't a numeric value and so "absent >= absent" is false.

I prefer the first option as it preserves the usual law that "x >= y" if and only if "x >y" OR "x ==y". (I guess we might want to add such laws to the spec too!)

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body: I, too, prefer the first option.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body: If your model is Javascript and "absent" has the same properties as "undefined", then inequality operators wouldn't be supported. If your model is a language that supports the notion of "optional", I can't think of any that support inequality operators for values of that type. But on this, the draft really needs to define its type system more precisely, as introducing the notion of "absent" extends the type system beyond JSON.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
According to the spec, the results of singular paths are nodelists consisting of at most one node. So one way to address this issue would be to say that:

* when a nodelist consisting of a single node appears in a comparison, it is replaced by the value of the node, and
* when an empty nodelist appears in a comparison, the result of the comparison is true if and only if the comparison is being made with another empty nodelist and the comparison operation is `==`, `>=` or `<=`.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body: You also have to think about what it means for an expression that evaluates to "absent" to be passed to a function (assuming the draft supports functions.) By comparison, in Javascript, a value of type undefined is passed to the function.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
> You also have to think about what it means for an expression that evaluates to "absent" to be passed to a function (assuming the draft supports functions.) By comparison, in Javascript, a value of type undefined is passed to the function.

Noted in https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/203#issuecomment-1168095582.
