Good idea. I added an example in af06ecf5e3c32f28156d2a39fd9d1ecfd354e5fa and also talk about "the value of a node" rather than suddenly talking about "the JSON value of a node" which seems a little distracting. See what you think.
I'd rather have `!=` `<` `>` be defined as the opposite of `==` `>=` `<=`.

Yes, I have a lot of sympathy for that. Before I make the change, let's see if there is a consensus for https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/212#issuecomment-1186563259 as this may be relevant here.

Consider a path `p` which results in an empty nodelist. Then according to the spec, `p <= 1` and `p >= 1` yield false.

If we define `>`, `<` as the negation of the operators `<=`, `>=`, respectively, then `p > 1` and `p < 1` yield true. This breaks the normal partial order laws (`p < 1` implies `1 > p`, but then we have `1 > p` and `p > 1`, which breaks the asymmetry law that if `a < b` then not `b < a`).

Instead, I'm thinking of keeping any path `p` which results in an empty nodelist **outside** the partial order. Thus `p <= 1`, `p >= 1`, `p > 1`, and `p < 1` would all yield false (as would `p < p` and `p > p`, as expected).

Please see 20f1d84bcb79ec088a4f06dcc2a697352ad6b606 for an attempt at this approach.

The options under consideration in issue [212](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/212) were:

1. [The current draft as of 2022-07-22](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/blob/59b20529af450fc9d9a00179b95a6ae5bbe56de0/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base.md#comparisons).

3. [The NaB proposal](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/212#issuecomment-1186563259).
4. The NaB proposal, but with left-to-right evaluation and short-circuiting.
5. The option of forcing a total order among all values, like Erlang does.
6. The option of not selecting the current item if any type-mismatched comparisons occur anywhere in the expression.

This is option 2 with string comparisons.

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
On 28. Jul 2022, at 00:19, Greg Dennis ***@***.***> wrote:
> 
> This brings up an interesting point. JSON requires that UTF-16 characters

(Do you mean beyond-BMP characters?)

> be encoded in \uxxxx pairs.

You do not need to encode beyond-BMP characters, but if you do, you indeed go through UTF-16 surrogate pairs.

> Is the encoding sufficient to determine correct ordering (i.e. does sorting by the encoded strings yield the same result as sorting the unencoded characters)?

No, and that is true of other backslash-encoded characters, too.

You can sort by Unicode Scalar Values.
You can also sort by UTF-32 code units (obviously) and by UTF-8 code units (a.k.a. bytes) — UTF-8 was careful to preserve sorting order.

Grüße, Carsten

I'm happy to discuss this next week, but please note that:
* implementations are not **required** to use recursion (e.g. they could use a loop and allocate memory in a data structure),

No.

ECMA-404, and, to a lesser extent, RFC 8259 describe the format on the wire (JSON texts), which is where they couldn’t (or didn’t want to) summon the energy to exclude members with identical keys.

pulls.title: Ordered comparisons (<, >) of arrays
pulls.author: glyn
pulls.body:
Ordered comparisons of arrays are closely modelled on ordered
comparisons of strings, but if either array has a descendent of an
unordered type, the comparison yields false.

Added a note about slimming down the comparison examples table.

Fixes https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/244

Reviewers may find this [rendered version](https://ietf-wg-jsonpath.github.io/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/244-array-ordering/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base.html#name-comparisons) useful.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body: **Reviewers please note:** I intend to make an improvement if/when this PR lands: see https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/249. Since the improvement may make the text longer, I'd like to work with the current text while we decide whether we want to support ordered comparisons of strings at all. If this PR is merged, I'd then like to fix https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/249 in a similar way for strings and arrays.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
The reason for the restriction that array comparisons yield false if either array has a descendant which is an object, a boolean, or `null` is that without this restriction, transitivity is broken. For example, without this restriction `[0, true] < 1` would yield true as would `1 < [2, 1]`. If `<` was to remain transitive, then `[0, true] <  [2, 1]` would yield false, but it would actually yield false because the comparison fails on the second element.

(I am thinking of adding a note to the text about this to clarify the rationale.)

* `'ab' < 'abc'` yields `true`, but `['a','b'] < ['a','b','c']` will yield `false` ... 
* how to deal with nested arrays and possible edge cases ?
* why not use [product order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_order)  `[a,b] < [c,d]  if  a<c and b<d` instead ?

The benefit for users is questionable at best (I would like to get some use cases documented) ... while the effort for implementers (and spec writers :-) is significant.

So I propose ...
1. to allow general relations `==,!=,<,>,<=,>=` for numbers and strings.
2. comparison of all other types support `==, !=` and yield `false` otherwise (mixed types!).

... as long as no strong demand from users and/or implementers is heard.

What is your concern? That the definition is hard to understand? That we might tempt implementers to use recursion? Or something else?

I also think it could influence implementors.

I already stated in interim meeting, that I do have objections against `</>` comparisons of different arrays.

## Arrays containing Numbers only

With arrays (seen as vectors mathematically) mostly a distinct meaning of members is implied:
* `[x,y,z]`  ... Spatial vector.
* `[r,g,b]` ... RGB color.

There is no  linear order in the plane, in the space or in any n-dimensional structure. So with the rgb color example, we won't say, that `blue` is smaller than `green` or `green` is smaller than red, i.e. `[0,0,255] < [0,255,0]`.

Of course, we could apply lexicographical ordering here, but many people would be confused by this.  In fact there is a lexicographical [ordering of vector spaces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordered_vector_space) defined. But from my experience in math and geometry it is of rare practical use. 

Only looking at complex numbers, which can be seen as planar vectors `[a,b]` [ordering them](https://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~angell/articles/complexorder.pdf) is proofed as [not possible](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/487997/total-ordering-on-complex-numbers).

The same applies to an array of strings. there must be a reason not to create a single string here.

## Arrays containing no Numbers, no Strings exclusively

I think we all agree on the fact that the relation `<` or `>` always should yield false.

> I already stated in interim meeting, that I do have objections against `</>` comparisons of different arrays.
> ## Arrays containing Numbers only

It is [possible](https://shaileshk.medium.com/an-order-on-complex-numbers-6357c8b4aec2) to define a total order on complex numbers if you regard them as merely equivalent to planar vectors. The above proof that this cannot be done uses the "field" properties of complex numbers, such as `i*i = -1`.

pulls.title: Redefine <= and >=
pulls.author: glyn
pulls.body:
Changes:
* Frame `<=` in terms of `<` or `==`
* Frame `>=` in terms of `>` or `==`

comments.author: glyn
comments.body: Closing since superseded by https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/266 which is effectively the same change applied to a base which has moved on.
Recursive, instead of reflexive?

No - I deliberately borrowed the mathematical term "reflexive" because the nodelist includes the node itself.

The definition of _descendant_ is already recursive:

> Descendants (of a node): The children of the node, together with the children of its children, and so forth recursively. More formally, the descendants relation between nodes is the transitive closure of the children relation.

What we have here is the node and its descendants. This is the reflexive closure of the descendants relation. Or, putting it another way, it's the reflexive transitive closure of the children relation. Of course, there's the extra condition about the various possible orderings of the nodelist.

Is there a better phrase?

I still don't think "reflexive" is quite right.

> a binary relation R on a set X is reflexive if it relates every element of X to itself

Most significantly "descendants" (or even a "reflexive descendant") is not a binary relation.

It seems like a stretched attempt to come up with a single phrase when maybe it didn't need to be.

Maybe we just update the "descendants" definition to include the node.  Is there any time we use it to mean strictly children?

The binary relation I had in mind is "is a descendant of" which is a relation on JSON values and is the transitive closure of the "is a child of" relation. I considered redefining "descendants" to include the value itself, but that messes up the current descendants selectors because they only select strict descendants of the input value (NB. we don't currently support `..` on its own).

I have pushed a commit which avoids introducing a special term. See if that helps.

> Maybe we just update the "descendants" definition to include the node. Is there any time we use it to mean strictly children?

Yes, we decided in the past that "descendants" are children and children of children, not the node itself.

> No - I deliberately borrowed the mathematical term "reflexive" because the nodelist includes the node itself.
> 
> The definition of _descendant_ is already recursive:
> 
> > Descendants (of a node): The children of the node, together with the children of its children, and so forth recursively. More formally, the descendants relation between nodes is the transitive closure of the children relation.
> 
> What we have here is the node and its descendants. This is the reflexive closure of the descendants relation. Or, putting it another way, it's the reflexive transitive closure of the children relation. Of course, there's the extra condition about the various possible orderings of the nodelist.
> 
> Is there a better phrase?

XPath 3.1 uses [descendant-or-self](https://www.w3.org/TR/xpath-31/#unabbrev).

JSONAta uses [a few extra words](https://docs.jsonata.org/path-operators#-descendants) to explain

If the draft is targeting an audience of users, "reflexive" may not be the best choice.
@danielaparker Please see the updated PR which avoids "reflexive".

This is an interesting change and brings up and interesting point.

`.*` doesn't select the current node, only immediate children.  Now I'm questioning whether `..*` should select the current node.  I'll need to think about this some.

The comparison project shows a consensus for `..*` _not_ including the current node. See [this test](https://cburgmer.github.io/json-path-comparison/results/dot_notation_with_wildcard_after_recursive_descent.html).
I think only including children is the right way.  I can't think of an example where it'd be necessary to include the current node, and it has similarity with `.*` this way.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
Thanks for your comments @timbray and @gregsdennis. I feel I should explain. The current draft defines the orderings `<` and `>` using the same text. For strings, the text talks about "less than" but not "greater than". So the current text implicitly assumes that for strings `a` and `b`, `a > b` if and only if `b < a`. Non-mathematicians would tend to say this is patently obvious. But this PR avoids that assumption by only defining `<` using the same text and then defining `>` in terms of `<`.

However, I take the point about the standalone definitions and the arbitrariness of defining one in terms of the other.

So my question is: is the current draft text sufficiently precise? If not, I'll rework this PR to make it more precise. (When I started out doing that, it began to get quite wordy, so I changed tack.)

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
To summarize my stance:

*Pickers are the actors within the Child Selector, which merely functions as an aggregator.  If you want to think of the *pickers as simply _identifying_ (or matching) which children to select, then sure.  It makes no difference really.  This is the crux of the relationship between them.

@glyn has failed to explain why he feels that *pickers or their semantics are not sufficiently defined.  I've not changed much of the text; I've merely moved it around a bit.

There is also a debate around iteration.  Either the selector or the *picker must do iteration.  For me, it doesn't make sense for the selector to do the iteration because the only *picker that needs iteration is the filter *picker.  The other *pickers (index, name, slice) don't need to iterate through the values to identify which ones to *pick.  Only the filter needs to do this.  Because of this asymmetry, it only makes sense to have the filter *picker iterate.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
@glyn I've realized that we may have had a conflict of communication earlier regarding iteration.  I'd like to expand on that.

There are two kinds of iteration happening:

- input nodelist iteration
- child iteration

The way I see it, the child selector will perform the first kind, input nodelist iteration.  It iterates over the nodelist resulting from the previous selector, passing each node to each of the *pickers.  (This is the iteration I now think you may have been referring to.)

Each *picker then identifies which children of that node that the child selector should return.  Filter *pickers, specifically, must iterate over the children of the node in order to make this determination.  The other *pickers do not need to iterate of the children; they can merely use the bounds. (This is the iteration I was referring to.).

A couple examples:

- `0:5:2` would be given a node (as part of the nodelist iteration from the selector).  If that node is an array, then it just returns the values at indices 0, 2, and 4, if those indices exist.  I see this as direct access (think array access in C), not iteration.
- `?@.foo==1` would also be given a node.  This *picker would need to iterate over and evaluate all of the children of the node in order to identify which ones are objects where the `foo` property is `1`.

The *picker identifies which children to select from a single node as the child selector iterates over the previous nodelist.  The *picker then identifies which children of that node to select.  Finally, the child selector aggregates those children (via concatenation) and outputs them in its own nodelist for consumption by the next selector (or for path output).

## Ordering

The order of the resulting node list is the full selection of each *picker across the entire nodelist concatenated in the order of the *pickers.

```json
[
  [ "a1", "b1", "c1", "d1" ],
  [ "a2", "b2", { "foo": 2 }, "d2" ],
  [ "a3", "b3", "c3", { "foo": 3 } ],
  [ "a4", "b4", "c4", "d4" ]
]
```

```jsonpath
$[*][1,?@.foo]
```

The `[*]` returns the arrays in its nodelist:

- `[ "a1", "b1", "c1", "d1" ]`
- `[ "a2", "b2", { "foo": 2 }, "d2" ]`
- `[ "a3", "b3", "c3", { "foo": 3 } ]`
- `[ "a4", "b4", "c4", "d4" ]`

Then the child selector passes each one of those to the *pickers.

- From `[ "a1", "b1", "c1", "d1" ]`
    - `1` identifies `"b1"`
    - `?@.foo` identifies nothing
- From `[ "a2", "b2", { "foo": 2 }, "d2" ]`
    - `1` identifies `"b2"`
    - `?@.foo` identifies `{ "foo": 2 }`
- From `[ "a3", "b3", "c3", { "foo": 3 } ]`
    - `1` identifies `"b3"`
    - `?@.foo` identifies `{ "foo": 3 }`
- From `[ "a4", "b4", "c4", "d4" ]`
    - `1` identifies `"b4"`
    - `?@.foo` identifies nothing

But we need this in *picker order, so we take all of the results from `1` followed by all of the results from `?@.foo`.  The resulting nodelist from the child selector is:

- `"b1"`
- `"b2"`
- `"b3"`
- `"b4"`
- `{ "foo": 2 }`
- `{ "foo": 3 }`

The resulting list could also be achieved using multiple iterations of the input nodelist, passing all of them to each picker in turn.  This would avoid the re-sorting step at the end.  Either algorithm is fine with me, they're both O(n²).  If you think one is easier to comprehend, let's use that.

I'm not sure how much of this you want laid out in the document.

@gregsdennis I suspect we have quite different ideas of what constitutes a spec. From my perspective, the purpose of the JSONPath spec is to describe _what_ the results (plural because of non-determinism) can be, given a JSON value and a JSONPath, but without prescribing _how_ the results are computed.

Occasionally, it's necessary to write parts of the spec as an algorithm, such as the details of slicing, because the behaviour is just too "fiddly" to write as a non-algorithmic spec. But this is not meant to dictate how all implementations should be written - any implementation which produces equivalent results is acceptable.

> But we need this in *picker order, so we take all of the results from `1` followed by all of the results from `?@.foo`. The resulting nodelist from the child selector is:
>

The current draft has a [top-level semantics section](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/blob/36cdd27cd14e07318aa801039a34710ebb1a72be/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base.md#semantics) which describes, admittedly in somewhat algorithmic terms, the nodelists passed between the selectors constituting a JSONPath. This section is unmodified in the current PR. I think this is really the only place which needs to deal with what you describe as iterating over the nodelist. Individual selectors just need to say what their output nodelist can be for any input value (i.e. just one element of the input nodelist).

The other iteration you describe involves the children of one of the input values of the child selector. That's the one I had in mind when I described [two options](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/258#discussion_r967854964) for how to specify the selector-*picker interface. I believe those options are equivalent as specifications of _what_ the results of a child selector can be. We don't want to mandate either option as the way implementations should be written. Indeed, some implementations could be structured as selectors and *pickers and other implementations could have only selectors.

So how do we choose which option to use in the spec? Not by the performance of a naive implementation which mirrors the structure of the spec closely, since more optimal implementations are perfectly acceptable so long as they produce results which conform to the spec.

We should choose the option which gives the clearest specification. This is a value judgement. I preferred option 2 because its interface is narrower in the sense that it deals with a single child of the input value. The ordering of the children is then not a concern for *pickers. Of course, a naive implementation of option 2 could perform badly, e.g. when applying an index *picker to a value with a great many children, but other implementations could avoid unnecessary iteration.

However, you preferred option 1 and I was comfortable going along with that, so long as we understand that the goal is to write a spec rather than prescribe how implementations should be written. With option 1, each *picker is really a selector because it takes a value (from its input nodelist) and produces a nodelist. This means that the current selector text can be largely reused. Instead of the *picker descriptions being reworked to talk about matching, I think it's fine (in option 1) to simply say which children each *picker selects, and the order in which these occur in the output nodelist.

With option 2, the multi-child aspects can all be described in the child selector spec. Each *picker spec just needs to describe whether or not a given child is matched, which from my perspective is quite a lot simpler.

Does this help? Sorry for a long answer, but as you appreciate, it's easy to miscommunicate.

_Edited to correct the option numbering._

comments.body:
Notes for making changes discussed in the recent interim meeting.

---

The way the document is organized before I made changes today has the "root selector" as a subsection of **Selectors**.  In the meeting, we had recognized that while the output of `$` is a nodelist, it is not itself a selector, and we decided on the name "starter," following the placeholder *starter that @cabo had proposed.

While working on this, I moved this subsection to its own `<h2>` before the *pickers section.  In doing so, calling it a "starter" felt strange.  I've used "root identifier" instead, and I think the text reads a bit better.

Additionally, I searched for the other *starter `@` (for current-item relative paths), and found that it's defined within the "filter *picker" section.  I think this makes sense since it only has context there, but I can move it to a subsection alongside `$` if others think that's warranted.

---

There is no term definition for "selector," even though it's used in the definition for "Singular Path."  I can add one (as "appender"), if needed.

---

After making the selector -> appender change, I'm not really sure I like the term "appender," but I don't really have anything else for it.  I'm continuing to think on this, but "appender" will suffice for now.

The picker -> selector change reads _really_ well in my opinion.

---

I'm not sure about the ordering of sections

```
3.4 Root Identifier
3.5 Selectors
    3.5.1 Wildcard
    3.5.2 Name
    3.5.3 Index
    3.5.4 Slice
    3.5.5 Filter
3.6 Appenders
    3.6.1 Child
    3.6.2 Descendant
```

I think it would be better if we do  `Root ... Appender ... Selector` order.  The idea behind this is:

- It follows the order in which you encounter the syntax in a path: `$['name'].  You get the root first, then an appender, then a selector
- It's analogous to year-month-day in that you start broad and get narrower scopes as you go.

I'd like to get others' opinions here.

```suggestion
The resulting nodelist of a child selector with a single //PICKER// applied to a value is the collection of children of the value matched by the //PICKER//. If the value is an array, the resultant nodelist is in array order. If the value is an object, the order of the resultant nodelist is not stipulated, since JSON objects are unordered. If the value is a primitive JSON value (a number, a string, true, false, or null), the resulting nodelist is empty.

The resulting nodelist of a child selector with more than one //PICKER// is the concatenation of
the nodelists which would result from child selectors containing each of its //PICKERS//. The order of the nodelists to be concatenated is the same as the order of the //PICKERS// in the original child selector.

Without constraining implementations, I think we should define the processing model for how selectors and *pickers work together. I think there is a choice between:

1. a selector presents a single value to a *picker, the *picker matching zero or more children of the value, and the selector builds its resultant node list from the matched children (plus some words about concatenating the node lists together when there is more than one *picker), and
2. a selector presents each child of a value in turn to a *picker along with the value's name (if the value is a child of an object) or index (if the value is a child of an array), the *picker matches the value or doesn't match the value, and the selector builds its resultant node list from the matched children (plus some words about concatenating the node lists together when there is more than one *picker).

I _think_ the behaviour is equivalent in either case. The choice simply influences how each *picker is specified (and how each selector which uses *pickers is specified). I personally favour option 2 because it makes the *picker interface narrower and I think that will make the *picker specs shorter and simpler.

> As you can see from the diff, I didn't change this text.

No, but perhaps you should have. See https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/258#discussion_r967854964 for why.

> 
> I'm not sure how the result being a nodelist confuses *pickers and selectors given that the result of the child selector is exactly the concatenation of the *pickers it contains.

If the result of a *picker was simply a boolean (match or didn't match), there would be a clearer distinction between selectors and *pickers.

> > The resulting nodelist of a child selector with a single //PICKER// applied to a value is the collection of children of the value matched by the //PICKER//.
> 
> I don't think it's necessary to call out operation of the selector with a single *picker.

I don't see how the behaviour is well defined if we leave this out. It seems to me that the spec is silent on this matter.

> 
> > If the value is an array, the resultant nodelist is in array order. If the value is an object, the order of the resultant nodelist is not stipulated, since JSON objects are unordered.
> 
> This is addressed in the *pickers that can select multiple values (slice & filter). I don't think it makes sense outside of that context. The operation here isn't precisely value selection; it's concatenating the results of the *pickers.

I checked the text of the filter *picker and it doesn't specify the result order. It talks about iterating, but doesn't tie down the order of iteration. (Also I, like @goessner, would prefer to avoid implementation terms like iteration.)
Fair enough, but shuffling the order makes it harder to review the changes.
We already define the terms "children" and "descendants" in the terminology section.
The phrase "select some or all of the descendants" is sufficient without needing to talk about recursively selecting.
Ok, it's an editorial change rather than something substantive.

How about this?
```suggestion
The two formats, `index-wild-selector` and `dot-wild-selector`,
are semantically identical.
```

It's only sufficient if we define "descendants" to mean all of them down the tree (which apparently we have, and recursively)

(line 222)
```
Children (of a node):
: If the node is an array, each of its elements,
  or if the node is an object, each of its member values (but not its
  member names). If the node is neither an array nor an object, it has no children.

Descendants (of a node):
: The children of the node, together with the children of its children, and so forth
  recursively. More formally, the descendants relation between nodes is the transitive
  closure of the children relation.
```

I can change this here since "descendants" is defined as such.
Yes, it does.  Let's hold for a secondary PR.
I think it's worth explicitly stating their interchangeability.

> I don't see how the behaviour is well defined if we leave this out. It seems to me that the spec is silent on this matter.

A single item is just a list of length one.  That's the basis of this PR.  Since how a list of *pickers works is defined, a single *picker is inherently defined.

> I checked the text of the filter *picker and it doesn't specify the result order. It talks about iterating, but doesn't tie down the order of iteration.

Okay.  I prefer to add it there rather than in the selector because not all *pickers iterate, only the filter one does.

> Also I, like @goessner, would prefer to avoid implementation terms like iteration.

We need some description of going over each item in turn.  How else would you say this aside from "iterate"?

The numeric index *picker `1` doesn't have a boolean result.  It has a value result.  The slice *picker has a set of values as a result.  Similarly, the filter *picker has a set of values as a result.

Saying a *picker has a boolean result may work for filters, but it doesn't work for the other *pickers.  This confuses what a *picker is.

My thinking is in line with the first option.

Suppose we have `$[1]` and the data is an array with 1000 items.  It doesn't make sense to describe the selector as presenting each item to the *picker `1` to get a boolean result to determine whether to include it.

> the *picker matches the value or doesn't match the value

A *picker can't do this from just the value.  The `1` in my example needs the context of position within its parent.  _Filters_ specifically function just on the value, but the others don't.  Thus is wrong to generalize this way.

> My thinking is in line with the first option.
> 
> Suppose we have `$[1]` and the data is an array with 1000 items. It doesn't make sense to describe the selector as presenting each item to the *picker `1` to get a boolean result to determine whether to include it.

Why not? This is a specification and doesn't imply that an implementation would do the same.

> 
> > the *picker matches the value or doesn't match the value
> 
> A *picker can't do this from just the value. The `1` in my example needs the context of position within its parent.

That's why option 2 says that the value's name or index is also provided to the *picker.

> _Filters_ specifically function just on the value, but the others don't. Thus is wrong to generalize this way.

Not necessarily. If the value and its name/index is passed to the *picker, that provides enough context for all *pickers. Some may ignore some of these "parameters", but again we are talking about a spec rather than an implementation.
Not necessarily. Option 2 allows other *pickers to function correctly because they can use the name or index of the value as part of their spec.

> > I don't see how the behaviour is well defined if we leave this out. It seems to me that the spec is silent on this matter.
> 
> A single item is just a list of length one. That's the basis of this PR. Since how a list of *pickers works is defined, a single *picker is inherently defined.

Not so, I'm afraid. Please could you point me to the text which says how a selector with a single *picker operates.

> 
> > I checked the text of the filter *picker and it doesn't specify the result order. It talks about iterating, but doesn't tie down the order of iteration.
> 
> Okay. I prefer to add it there rather than in the selector because not all *pickers iterate, only the filter one does.
> 
> > Also I, like @goessner, would prefer to avoid implementation terms like iteration.
> 
> We need some description of going over each item in turn. How else would you say this aside from "iterate"?

We can use phrases like "the *picker matches certain values in the array". The spec only needs to say what the result is, not how the result is arrived at.

> Why not? This is a specification and doesn't imply that an implementation would do the same.

For the same reason we try not to prescribe implementation: implementors will default to the process described in the spec.  If the spec describes a known bad way to do something, that's bad for implementors.

It just doesn't make sense to have the iteration done at the selector when ONLY ONE *picker actually does any kind of iteration.  Filter is the only picker that iterates over the values.  It's also the only one that depends on the value at all.  All of the others depend on the value's location in relation to its parent.

**It's incorrect to describe this behavior holistically because there is no holistic behavior among the *pickers.**

You want to define the relationship between selectors and *pickers.  Here you go:

> The child selector selects values identified by the *pickers it contains by concatenating the resulting sets of values from each *picker in the order they appear without removing duplicates.

The *picker identifies which values to select, and the selector "selects" them.  Yeah, the child selector is little more than a container for *pickers.  That's okay.  It doesn't have to do anything.

reviews.author: glyn
reviews.body:
I think it's time other reviewers weighed in, but let me summarise where I stand as the conversations in the PR are meandering somewhat.

The main benefit of this PR seems to be to unify certain parts of the syntax. This may make the spec easier for implementers to read.

However, thus far, //PICKERS// seem to add little semantic value over selectors. Both produce nodelists and the distinction between //PICKERS// and selectors appears to be mainly syntactic.

An alternative approach ([option 2](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/258#discussion_r967854964)) defines //PICKERS// in terms of matching with a boolean outcome. This would make a clean semantic distinction between //PICKERS// and selectors. This approach was rejected.

I have the following concerns:
* //PICKERS// don't pull their weight (as described above)
* the selector-//PICKERS// interface is not yet defined sufficiently clearly,
* the general semantics of //PICKERS// is not yet defined sufficiently clearly,
* the resultant document is less readable for users than the current draft because they have to deal with an extra //PICKER// term which doesn't add much value and because the document structure is more deeply nested.

PSt: As I ponder this PR further, one of the things I struggle with is the fact that //PICKERS// act on just the children of the input node, matching or selecting zero or more of them. So //PICKERS// only really make sense in the context of a selector which operates on children/descendants. Lifting //PICKERS// out to be a first class concept inevitably requires them to be biassed toward matching or selecting children. I feel as if we want to identify //PICKERS// _syntactically_ but define their semantics only in terms of the context of selectors. If we could do that, we might obtain the main benefits of this PR without the downsides.

PPS: I wonder if the approach of documenting syntax and semantics of constructs "side by side" is part of the problem here. It seems this PR is introducing a better syntactic structure, but perhaps we could organise the semantics differently? Just a thought, rather than a conclusion.

reviews.author: glyn
reviews.body:
@gregsdennis ok, here are some actionable changes which I think follow your preferred approach and should satisfy the concerns which I and others have raised. If you would like some help implementing these changes because it's not clear what I have in mind, I'd be happy to assist. My hope is that we can then achieve consensus, choose a term for __PICKER__, and merge the PR.

1. Define __PICKER__ as a kind of selector which takes a value and produces a nodelist. (And remove the current definition "A single item within a bracketed (`[]`) child selector that matches the values which are to be selected." which is focused on one example of how __PICKERS__ are used.)
2. State that __PICKERS__ are used to construct other selectors, but cannot be used on their own. Any selector which uses a __PICKER__ must define the __PICKER__'s input value and what is done with the __PICKER__'s output nodelist.
3. Move the __PICKER__ sections before those of the other selectors in the document to minimise forward references, reduce section nesting, and improve readability.
4. Introduce the __PICKER__ sections by describing the general semantics of __PICKERS__ and the selector-__PICKER__ interface (bullets 1 and 2 above).
This section should also include ABNF which lists the possible __PICKER__ types.
5. Revise the Child selector section to use the above language in its use of __PICKERS__.
6. Check the Descendant selector section uses the above language when it discusses __PICKERS__.

I imagine that __PICKER__ could be then replaced by some term such as "abstract selector", "dependent selector", "subselector", or such like. Terms like these would emphasise that __PICKERS__ are a kind of selector.

The introductory __PICKER__ section involves ABNF forward references, but we already do that when defining the `json-path` production. I think this is marginally better than drawing together the __PICKERS__ after all the __PICKER__sections, although that's another option.

I hope that requesting actionable changes will provide a constructive way forward. We may need to fine tune the result, but we might even be able to merge the PR and then deal with fine tuning in an editorial PR.

comments.author: glyn
comments.body: @cabo I'm going to merge this so I can progress other changes. I'd still appreciate your review and I will apply any fixes in a subsequent PR.
How does this example differ from the `..j` examples?

> How does this example differ from the `..j` examples?

The `$..j` example is unaffected by whether or not the input value is part of the enumeration. On the other hand, this example depends on that decision. If the input value was not part of the enumeration, then the resultant nodelist would be empty. So this example demonstrates that the input value is part of the enumeration.

I don't see how that's the case.  The `..j` examples pull the values at those locations. The `..o` example does the same thing.  It's just that the value for `..o` is an object.

I think it would be more apparent if you used `..*` to show that the current _and_ descendants are returned.

I wonder if the wording of the semantics section needs improving as it seems that you aren't reading it the same way as me.

There are two steps involved:

1. enumerating a nodelist of descendants _plus the input value_, and
2. applying the child segment corresponding to the descendant segment to that nodelist.

With that in mind, does my [previous comment](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/266#discussion_r996497750) now explain the need for the `$..o` example?

We could add a `$..*` example, but please note this would return just the descendants of the input value since step 2 would apply the child segment `$[*]` which returns all the children of each of its input values (and not the value itself).

BTW please note that table 2 already includes a `$..*` example with the result:

> all member values and array elements contained in input value

> With that in mind, does my previous comment now explain the need for the $..o example?

I'm sorry, I still don't understand why this example illustrates the change.  What would the result be without the change (or, what's the alternative interpretation of `..o`)?
To be clear, I agree that the input node should be included. I just don't understand how this example drives that point home.

> I'm sorry, I still don't understand why this example illustrates the change. What would the result be without the change (or, what's the alternative interpretation of `..o`)?

Without the change, the enumerated nodelist would be something like this:
* `{"j": 1, "k": 2}`
* `1`
* `2`
* `[5, 3, [{"j": 4}]]`
* `5`
* `3`
* `[{"j": 4}]`
* `4`

Applying the corresponding child segment `['o']` to this list produces the empty nodelist.

With the change, the enumerated nodelist would include: `{
  "o": {"j": 1, "k": 2},
  "a": [5, 3, [{"j": 4}]]
}` and so applying the corresponding child segment `['o']` produces the nodelist:
* `{"j": 1, "k": 2}`

Hmmm... I don't see the `..` operating separately from the `o`.  I see it all as a single step because it's defined that way in the syntax.

`..o` says, "navigate recursively (starting with the current node) and return nodes under `o` properties as you find them."  That immediately gives you 

```json
{ "j": 1, "k": 2 }
```

It doesn't say, "navigate recursively, give me all the nodes, _then from that_ give me the `o` properties."

I now see that you're changing the text to mean the two-step operation, but again, I think that conflicts with how the syntax is declared.

> The descendant segment consists of a double dot `..` followed by a child segment (`descendant-segment`).

and later

> Note that `..` on its own is not a valid segment.

This explicitly states that `..` carries no meaning by itself.  The `..` is inseparable from its associated child segment.  That means that the `..` _cannot_ produce a nodelist for the child segment to act upon; they _must_ act together.

I really think the simpler approach is to process the selectors _while_ enumerating the (recursive) descendants.  (I know that we're not pushing algorithms, but _something_ needs to be in the spec.)
Given my last two comments, I would say that the text (both as it was and your proposal) should be revisited.  They do both seem to convey the two-step process you've demonstrated.

I agree with Greg here: Just as a child segment offers `self` to the selectors, a descendants segment offers `self` and `descendant` to the selectors.  Having the `$..o` example to illustrate this is a good idea.

(Other examples need to be fixed if we stick with `"j j"` and `"k.k"`.)

Please see 17835689a97eae026254e7cc28197817cbfbcf21 in which I've expressed the semantics the way you suggest.

I believe the semantics are unchanged.
 
> (Other examples need to be fixed if we stick with `"j j"` and `"k.k"`.)

Not sure what this is referring to because the examples in this section mention neither `"j j"` nor `"k.k"`. However, I've pushed 20bb114990b615da55a7be662e5bb37e218182b7 which deletes the erroneous child selector examples.

> However, I've pushed 20bb114 which deletes the erroneous child selector examples.

Thanks.

I've reworked the text in c7f54040f56756c2dd10e05cebbaa0d1a8fb31c1 to make the semantics much more obvious.

Is it necessary to have the `.a` in here?  I thought we were trying to illustrate the multi-selector behavior.  It seems having the additional segment muddies the example.

```suggestion
Suppose the nodes, in the order visited, are `D1`, ..., `Dn` where `n >= 1`.
(Note that `D1` is the input value.)

For each node `Di` such that `1 <= i <= n`, the resulting nodelist `Ri` is defined to be a result of applying
the all of the selectors in the child segment `[<selectors>]` to the node `Di`.

The final result of the descendant selector is the concatenation of `R1`, ..., `Rn` (in that order).
```

I fear that

> Note that only a single traversal of the input value and its descendants is required.

may be getting too close to specifying implementation logic.

Ok, I'll delete the single traversal sentence.

I didn't adopt the proposal because it talks about applying all the selectors in the child segment, but we need child segment semantics (specifically, concatenating the selector nodelists) instead of just selector semantics.

My suggestion also provides a more precise wording and adjusts the parenthetical phrases.

> it talks about applying all the selectors in the child segment, but we need child segment semantics (specifically, concatenating the selector nodelists) instead of just selector semantics

Then I suggest we remove mention of the selectors completely.

```
Suppose the nodes, in the order visited, are `D1`, ..., `Dn` where `n >= 1`.
(Note that `D1` is the input value.)

For each node `Di` such that `1 <= i <= n`, the intermediate nodelist `Ri` is the result of applying
the child segment `[<selectors>]` to the node `Di`.

The result of the descendant segment is the concatenation of the intermediate nodelists `R1`, ..., `Rn` (in that order).
```

We also need to be sure that in the "child segment" section, we define how the selector results are concatenated, which it seems we do:

> The resulting nodelist of a child segment is the concatenation of the nodelists from each of its selectors in the order that the selectors appear in the list.

> Then I suggest we remove mention of the selectors completely.

As for the rest of the suggestion, I prefer the current wording in the PR:
* I prefer to define `Ri` via universal quantification over `i`, rather than over `Di`.
* I don't see any advantage in introducing the extra term "intermediate nodelist".

Are you comfortable with approving now?

> - I prefer to define Ri via universal quantification over i, rather than over Di.
> - I don't see any advantage in introducing the extra term "intermediate nodelist".

I'll take these as a difference of opinion.  I think that `Di` is the important variable here, not `i`.  And I added the "intermediate" qualifier to explicitly distinguish the `Ri`s as being partial results and not the final result of the descendant segment.
Thanks for explaining your opinions. I beg to differ. Is this still a blocker for you or can you now approve the PR?

Yes, but it's only an artefact of having a single JSON document and group of examples per section of examples. See https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/269/files#r998358723. Let's see how this reads later.

Well, we describe the nature of what it is to implement JSONPath.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
My [JsonPath.Net library](https://www.nuget.org/packages/JsonPath.Net) now implements everything in the spec, including this PR.  (It also supports math operations in expressions, which isn't part of the spec (yet).)

The function infrastructure was a struggle (mostly because I'm in a strongly typed language, I suspect), but once implemented, creating the functions themselves and registering them so that they can be parsed was easy!

With my lib, the user would implement a "function definition" interface which exposes the name, the range of parameters expected (min/max), and the logic for the function itself (which follows a pattern defined in my lib).  Once an instance of their definition is registered, it's available to be parsed.  The parsing logic handles validating that the function receives the correct number of parameters, too, so if you send `length()` seven arguments, it'll fail to parse.

This doesn't convert a singular path to a value.
`length($.foo)` would not work?

Correct, and that's too limiting. I was trying to avoid the issue a function expecting a value but receiving an empty nodelist from a singular path. Here are some alternatives if we allowed a singular path or a function expression returning a singular nodelist:

* We could coerce an empty nodelist to, for example, `null` at runtime, but we've managed to avoid coercions elsewhere in the spec.
* We could cause the filter not to match for the current item. This would impact the Boolean laws which would no longer be true in general.

Another alternative occurred to me. We could introduce a function extension `value_or_else()` which takes a singular nodelist and a default value and returns a value. The result would be the value of the node if the nodelist is non-empty and the default value otherwise. We could then use `length(value_or_null(<singular path>, ""))`. This is probably too long-winded to be practical.

Another alternative would be to define another `length()` function which takes a singular nodelist and which can be defined to return a suitable default (such as 0 or -1) if the nodelist is empty. Not sure we want to get into overloading of function extension names. That could be an issue for IANA.

I assume that with `length($.foo)` not working, we imply `$.foo` is taken as an existence test, right?

In the same way as an implementation needs to distinguish occurences of paths as part of comparisons or just not, they should be able to detect, if a path occurs as a function parameter and might be handed over as it is then. That way the burden/freedom to correctly treat the path lies at the function author (simply taking its value here with `length`).

Have I missed something here?

> I assume that with `length($.foo)` not working, we imply `$.foo` is taken as an existence test, right?

Oops.  That was not what I intended -- length wants an array, a map or a text string.
So converting this to a Boolean is not what one wants here.
(But for some other function extension, this might exactly be what is wanted -- however, this could then possibly be forced by `!!$.foo`.)
So maybe we need to distinguish function parameters where the arguments are evaluated in a comparison-like context, and parameters where the arguments are evaluated as an existence test.

Yes, `!!$.foo` would be perfectly fine in case of an existence test as parameter.

But ... exactly what prevents `length($.foo)` from working then?

@goessner The basic problem of defining `length($.foo)` when `$.foo` is the empty nodelist is that, currently, `length()` is defined to take a value (possibly from a singular path) and an empty nodelist isn't a value.

Perhaps a more drastic solution is to take a functional programming approach and define a type `OptionalNodeOrValue` with instances (using the term "values" would be too confusing in this context!) of:
* `None`,
* `Node(n)` for some node `n`, and
* `Value(v)` for some JSON value `v`.

These instances would be represented concretely, respectively, as:
* A singular path resulting in an empty nodelist,
* A singular path resulting in a nodelist with one node, and
* A value.

We would then specify the result of `length()` in each of these three cases.

So far, that doesn't gain us much. But if we allowed the result of a function to be of type `OptionalNodeOrValue`, we could then allow functions to compose together sensibly. For example, suppose we said the result of `length()` was of type `OptionalNodeOrValue`, then we could specify that if the input was `None`, then the result would be `None`. This gets us out of the game of using a special value, such as `0` or `-1`, to cover this case.

So are we not accepting functions which _may_ return a single value but _could_ return multiple values?

This could only be a runtime determination, so static syntactical analysis couldn't find it.  (I realize that's an argument against such functions; just clarifying.)

Static checks reduce the number of runtime errors we have to cope with in the spec, so I'd prefer to rule out that kind of function signature. However, if we allowed a function to return a list of values (which we currently don't), then such a function could return a list of size one.

Expanding on this functional programming approach, we could define the following types, where `Nodes(l)` is an instance for some nodelist `l` (which could be represented either as a path or as a nodelist):
* `OptionalNodeOrValue = {None, Node(n), Value(v)}`
* `OptionalNode = {None, Node(n)}`
* `OptionalValue = {None, Value(v)}`
* `Value = {Value(v)}`
* `Absent = {None}` (this may not be necessary, but allows, for example, a logging function with no return value)
* `OptionalNodes = {None, Nodes(l)}` (where `None` is equivalent to `Nodes(e)`, where `e` is the empty nodelist)

Each function argument  or return value would have one of the above types. 

The types form a hierarchy (with subtypes indented):
```
OptionalNodeOrValue
    OptionalNode
        Absent
    OptionalValue
        OptionalNode
        Value
        Absent
    Value
    Absent

OptionalNodes
    OptionalNode
        Absent
```

So, for example, a function with return value of type `Value` could be passed to another function with an argument of type `OptionalValue`.

Notes:
* `OptionalNode` is a subtype of `OptionalValue` even though the instances of the former are not a subset of the instances of the latter. The `OptionalNode` instance `Node(n)` can be coerced to the `OptionalValue` instance `Value(v)`, where `v` is the value of the node `n`.
* `OptionalNode` is a subtype of `OptionalNodes` even though the instances of the former are not a subset of the instances of the latter. The `OptionalNode` instance `Node(n)` can be coerced to the `OptionalNodes` instance `Nodes(l)`, where `l` is a nodelist consisting of just the node `n`.

What do people think of this approach?

This is far too abstract for me and perhaps for someone else.

From the view of an average user of JSONPath - knowing, there is a function `length`, familiar from C-family of languages - I would expect, that the query

`$[?length(@.something] >= 0]`

simply works regardless of the argument.

How would that query look like using your approach then?

I don't think we can avoid the inherent complexity.
Maybe we can slightly simplify the tree.

Defining this in an abstract way is fine for our specification.
Of course, a few examples can make this more accessible.

> How would that query look like using your approach then?

The query would be the same. I'm simply describing which function expressions are syntactically valid.

> Maybe we can slightly simplify the tree.

Note the type hierarchy (if that's the right word) isn't a tree since there are nodes such as `Value` with multiple parents.

> Of course, a few examples can make this more accessible.

For starters, here are some proposed signatures of the functions that are already in the spec:
* `length(OptionalNodeOrValue) -> OptionalValue`
* `count(OptionalNodes) -> Value`
* `match(Value) -> OptionalValue`
* `search(Value) -> OptionalValue`

For all these that return `OptionalValue`, `None` (i.e. an empty nodelist) is used in error cases (e.g. an empty nodelist argument to `length` or a non-string argument of `match` or `search`).

This makes it a bit clearer ... thanks. Also my example 

`$[?length(@.something] >= 0]`

seems to be in harmony with our comparison rules now.

comments.body:
Should this instead return `Nothing`?  We don't have any other cases where `Nothing` begets non-`Nothing`.  (You can't get something from nothing. 😆)

Also, to @cabo's point [here](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/392#issuecomment-1423289172), do we instead want to say that the input is just a nodelist (`NodesType`)?  I'm having trouble thinking of a scenario where it could actually get nothing.

`count`'s return type is `ValueType`, so `Nothing` would be invalid, but I suppose you are suggesting changing the return type to `OptionalValueType`.

However, `count` really should be dealing with nodelists (or functions that return the moral equivalent of a nodelist) and `Nothing` is simply an abstraction of an empty nodelist, so returning `0` seems consistent to me.

Sorry for the multiple conversations/option going here. I'll try to keep them separate.

---

> I suppose you are suggesting changing the return type to OptionalValueType.

Yes.  I'm suggesting this.

---

> `Nothing` is simply an abstraction of an empty nodelist

I'm not sure I agree with this.  So far, any expressions we have (except those which contain `count()`) that contains a `Nothing` currently evaluate to `Nothing`, which _yields_ an empty nodelist. It yields an empty nodelist because the expression is not evaluatable, so no nodes are selected.  But I wouldn't say one is an abstraction of the other.

The abstract vs concrete distinction is deliberate. The types and abstract instances are just that: abstract. They do not appear in code and they are not evaluated. Their purpose is to define the intended behaviour of the spec.

(Of course, implementations need to represent these abstractions somehow and are free to use algebraic data types, enumerated types, or such like that mirror the types and abstract instances in the spec so long as the resultant behaviour is equivalent.)

The spec describes a relationship between types with their abstract instances and concrete representations. It is the concrete representations that appear in code and which are evaluated.

Does that help?

No, it doesn't help. You're claiming that `Nothing` is an abstraction of the empty nodelist, but the spec doesn't say that, and I think it's incorrect.

`Nothing` was our placeholder for "no value." An empty nodelist is the output of a query that selected no nodes.   They're not the same thing.  They're not related.

> No, it doesn't help. You're claiming that `Nothing` is an abstraction of the empty nodelist, but the spec doesn't say that, and I think it's incorrect.

Er, the spec does say that. Table 14 says the abstract instance `Nothing` has concrete representations of a Singular Path or `filter-path` resulting in an empty nodelist.

> `Nothing` was our placeholder for "no value." An empty nodelist is the output of a query that selected no nodes. They're not the same thing. They're not related.

`Nothing` (initially named `Absent`) was inspired by earlier discussion of empty nodelists in the WG. [issue 123](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/123) (Is absent equal to absent?) gave rise to text describing [comparisons involving empty nodelists](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/207/files#diff-aca3bb236d11f768483f8a1153cb9030b67d9cd6a39f012e8e4bfec2c6275165R1227). That's why we chose those concrete representations in Table 14.

Well, we came from the observation that singular paths do not always return one node, but sometimes zero nodes.  So we started using the empty nodelist as our indicator of Nothing.  The next step was to also add Nothing to non-novelist types as a way to build an Optional type.  As I said, when you grew up on Lisp, that is very natural, as Lisp does exactly the same (() = nil).

But we *could* allow Nodes(nl) to carry an empty nodelist (which would remove the need to call Nodelists Optional).  We would introduce Nothing as a separate instance that is not an alternative to Nodelists, but an alternative to all other types that might otherwise be generated out of Nodes or Nodelists.  So these would have OptionalTTT (including a single OptionalNode).  OptionalNode can then be converted into Nodelist (Nothing ➔ empty NL, Node ➔ singular NL).  I think this could be made consistent.

Assumption here is that an empty Nodelist is always a good way to indicate failure for functions that return nodelists.  Since that is the overall semantics of JSONPath selectors, I think that is a tenable assumption.
(Just checking if this alternative world is maybe more acceptable for someone who did not evolve Lactose tolerance by continually being fed with Lisp.)

Table 13 defines `OptionalNodesType` as a nodelist or `Nothing`.  Why have this type at all if `Nothing` is just the empty nodelist?

If `Nothing` is the same as the empty nodelist, then `Nothing` is already a member of `Nodes(nl)`, and we should just have a `NodesType` for nodelists that's represented by `Nodes(nl)` without any mention of `Nothing`.

> Table 13 defines `OptionalNodesType` as a nodelist or `Nothing`. Why have this type at all if `Nothing` is just the empty nodelist?
> 
> If `Nothing` is the same as the empty nodelist, then `Nothing` is already a member of `Nodes(nl)`, and we should just have a `NodesType` for nodelists that's represented by `Nodes(nl)` without any mention of `Nothing`.

Actually, `Nodes(nl)` is defined as a non-empty nodelist.

```
| `Nodes(nl)`       | `filter-path` resulting in the non-empty nodelist `nl`             |
```

So Nothing is needed to complement this to a Type that includes all nodelists `OptionalNodeType`.
Not sure that this little piece of gymnastic really helps a lot, except that it underscores the Nothingness of the empty list...

Okay.  The distinction is found just above the row in Table 14 that you referenced:

> | `Nothing` | Singular Path or filter-path resulting in an empty nodelist |

`Nothing` _results_ in an empty nodelist, but it is not itself an empty nodelist.  You're saying that this means `Nothing` is _representative_ of an empty nodelist.

I could be okay with this if the text (above, in the PR) said something more along the lines of 

> If the argument is `Nothing` (which can represent an empty nodelist), the result is the value `0`.

But I'm still a little bothered that we're going from `Nothing` to a value.  This doesn't happen anywhere else, not even the logical NOT operator `!` does this.  (It reinterprets/casts `Nothing` as TestBoolean-false and inverts that to TestBoolean-true.)
I would be very happy, if we could get rid of that 'Nothing' thing somehow.

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
> Whether or not functions (and/or paths) returning non-singular nodelists should be allowed in comparisons.

From the ABNF, paths that return multiple nodes are not allowed in comparisons.  I agree with this, and this PR is not changing it.

From the type system, as described here, functions that return multiple nodelists are allowed in comparisons.  I think this is fine _with the defined conversions_ (also see below).  To change this, we would need to (one of):

- disallow nodelist functions in comparisons at all
- define a new type that represents a single-node nodelist that _is_ suitable for comparisons
- (there's also a third option)

## Disallow nodelist function in comparisons

I'm okay with this.  I'm not sure if this would limit any functionality, though.  It would limit functions that return `NodesType` to logicals because the nodelist is still convertible to (or "has meaning in," or however you want to say it) a logical.

The [examples](https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/402#issuecomment-1437796107) I put up for the hypothetical `distinct()` function were contrived to endure @cabo's tests.  I certainly can't think of a practical use case to put a nodelist in a comparison.

This does raise the question of whether to even have `NodesType`, though.  If a function that returns `NodesType` is only valid as a logical, then it might as well return `BooleanType`.

## Define a new type for single-node nodelists

A function that returns a single-node nodelist would be valid in a comparison, but a function that returns `NodesType` would not.

This is really an extension of disallowing nodelist functions in comparisons, so all of that logic still applies (i.e. is `NodesType` still useful?).

Conversely, a function that returns the new single-node nodelist type would only be useful in a comparison (otherwise, we run into the same inconsistencies that I've been highlighting this whole time).  Because it's only useful in a comparison, it might as well just return the value of the single node, which is `ValueType`.  So why have it?

## The third option

Only allow nodelist functions to be parameters for other functions, i.e. disallow them from both logicals and comparisons.

This would only allow something like `$[?count(distinct(@.*))==42]`, which is arguably useful, but both `$[?distinct(@.*)]` and `$[?distinct(@.*)==42]` would be invalid.

---

> Whether the spec would be clearer if it avoided type conversions.

We cannot avoid type conversions.  They are implicit in the grammar.

To prove this, I'll exclude functions.

**All paths return nodelists.  They don't return logicals, and they don't return values.**  Singular paths, specifically, return a nodelist with a single value.

Paths are always allowed to act as logicals.  That is, there is a _conversion_ from a nodelist to a logical.  Namely, if a nodelist has one or more nodes, it is treated as (converted to) `LogicalTrue`; if it has no nodes, it is treated as (converted to) `LogicalFalse`.  If I were to write `$[?@.a]` as a test expression explicitly (in a C-ish syntax), it would be:

```
$[?(LogicalType)@.a]
```

where I'm "casting" the nodelist returned by `@.a` to `LogicalType`.

Paths are allowed to act as values if they're singular.  That is, there is a _conversion_ from a nodelist to a value if the nodelist contains at most a single node.  If the nodelist were to contain more than one node, the conversion would be undefined, and a runtime error would occur.  To avoid the potential error, the ABNF applies an additional restriction to identify paths which are guaranteed to return at most a single node, and we can catch it at parse time.  Writing `$[?@.a==42]` explicitly would be:

```
$[?((ValueType)@.a)==42]  // extra parentheses not necessary, but can help readability
```

where I'm "casting" the nodelist returned by `@.a` to a `ValueType`.

We have specified these conversions by instead describing their behavior, but that doesn't detract from the fact that they're there.

Type conversions are unavoidable.  We might as well state them.  I think it helps us in the end.

Hey, I've been working on an implementation of this spec in Rust. Working with the specification has been a great experience. Now, I'm trying to follow these issues to see where things will land with the Functions Extension before I implement that part of the spec. I hope you don't mind me chiming in.

@gregsdennis - regarding the treatment of `@.path == 42` and `funcProducingNodelist(@.a) == 42` being equal...

My interpretation of the spec was that explicit conversion is not needed in the former case, because you are only allowed singular paths in comparisons.

So, a JSONPath containing `@.path[*]` or `@.path[1:10]`, or any other non-singular path in a comparison, would be rejected as invalid.

Writing a non-singular path into a comparison would require an explicit function invocation that produces a singular optional node from a nodelist, e.g., `first(@.path[*])` or `only_one(@.path[*])`. The same would be said for `funcProducingNodelist(...)`.

---

On the subject of this PR, I am okay with the idea that existence is implicit in cases like `$.path[?@.foo[*]]`, and forcing the use of a function like `exist` seems a bit awkward. This particular case is much like truthiness in JavaScript and a concept that I think is familiar to developers. Introducing the `exist` function seems to eliminate the need for *Existence Tests*.

An evolved function set, containing explicitly named functions that can perform these conversions, e.g., `is_empty`, `is_single_node`, etc., would allow users to make their queries more specific without any ambiguity.

pulls.title: Apply the same rules to function expressions as to non-function expressions
pulls.author: glyn
pulls.body:
By consistently applying the same rules for non-function expressions to function expressions, implicit type conversion (or at least such language) of function expressions and type conversion functions are not needed.

The rules are:
* Non-emptiness of nodelists constitutes an existence test in a test expression.
* A single-node nodelist represents the value of its node when used in comparisons.

This change increases referential transparency in that certain kinds of expressions with the same result may be used interchangeably.

Fixes https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/404
Fixes https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/issues/405

`SingleNodeType` is the only way to allow a function to be used both in a test expression and a comparison.  You were correct to introduce it.  If we make `match()` and `search()` return `SingleNodeType`, then both of these can be valid and work as expected:

```
$[?match(@.timezone, 'Europe/.*')]
$[?match(@.timezone, 'Europe/.*')==@.a]
```

If the match is found, it returns a single nodelist containing the value; otherwise it returns an empty nodelist.

- In a test expression, a found match evaluates to true, and no match evaluates to false.
- In a comparison, a found match evaluates to the matched value, and no match evaluates to `Nothing`.

I highly favor this, and this is the thing we were originally trying to solve anyway.

--

`value()` only requires the user to be explicit about the conversion.  The problems with having multiple-nodelists in comparisons still exist, and I shouldn't have put that in the text in the first place.  Doing so doesn't make sense.

If you still want to have a `value()` function, that's fine, but it needs to be separate from and not a replacement for `SingleNodeType`.

pulls.author: glyn

There are some syntactical representations, e.g.:

* LogicalTrue can be represented by (1==1).
* LogicalFalse can be represented by (1==0).
* Nothing can be represented by a query that always returns the empty nodelist, such as $[?1==0].

But these are somewhat circuitous rather than direct.

See https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/403#discussion_r1122546568

We create that registry in 3.2, so we can put a "Function Extensions sub-registry" there.
More IANA weirdness: there are registries (which map to webpages) and sub-registries inside these which are the actual registries (I'm not joking, there even is an RFC that complains these terms aren't very well-defined).
Please see the "CoRE Parameters registry" for an example.
JSONPath currently has only one sub-registry defined, which further adds to the confusion.
In evolving the spec, we might add sub-registries later under the roof of the "JSONPath Parameters registry".
https://www.iana.org/assignments/core-parameters/core-parameters.xhtml

Okay, so the actual registry for functions is the sub-registry, but JSON Path as a whole can have multiple sub-registries, so it must have a parent registry to hold the sub-registries.

Yep. Clear as mud.

Since we don't define what function overloading might be, this blanket statement could be interpreted to by itself rule out function registrations that allow several types for arguments to a parameter. pulls.title: add typed `function-expr`s to abnf
pulls.author: gregsdennis
pulls.body:
I was thinking the type system for functions could be reinforced somewhat using the ABNF.

This PR splits `function-expr` into three additional names that all just reference back to `function-expr`:

- `value-function-expr`
- `logical-function-expr`
- `nodes-function-expr`

I recognize that it's basically a no-op in the ABNF itself, but it gives us names that we can use in the text.  We do this elsewhere with rules like `start`, `end`, and `step` to define a slice selector; each of these all just reference `int`, but having them separate is handy.

Now that these have been added to the ABNF and have specific usages, we can reference them in the text to define them.  This prevents the need to use comments to specify what kind of function is valid.

We could go further and explicitly state which ABNF rule each function matches, but I don't think that's necessary.

There may be other places in the text where it says something like "a function with a result of `XType`," but I couldn't find any.

comments.body:
On 2023-04-20, at 07:19, Greg Dennis ***@***.***> wrote:
> 
> @cabo please explain why this isn't a good idea. It seems perfectly beneficial to me.

https://github.com/ietf-wg-jsonpath/draft-ietf-jsonpath-base/pull/416#discussion_r1125739805

The main argument was that these changes "need a painful hand-written parser with a lexer that assigns different syntactical categories based on a symbol table lookup, like in a C compiler. I'd like to stick with ABNF.”

Programming languages can be divided into those that can simply be parsed by a parser generator and those that require elaborate hand-crafting to intermingle semantic processing (symbol tables etc.) with parsing.  C and C++ are the latter.  JSONPath is the former.  I’d like it to stay in that class; absolutely no benefit is large enough to justify the damage that requiring this hand-crafting does.

Grüße, Carsten

comments.author: gregsdennis
comments.body:
@cabo, also note that my approach this time is inverted.  Instead of having the syntax all point to `function-name` where it splits out afterward (a definite problem), I'm now performing the split _before_ `function-expr`.  The funnel is inverted.

Last time:

```
                                            / --> value-function-name
expr --> function-expr --> function-name -------> logical-function-name
                                            \ --> nodes-function-name
```

There's no syntactical validation actually occurring here because regardless of context, you can still have any of the function names.

This proposal does actually have syntactical validation:

```
         / --> value-function-expr -----\
expr  -------> logical-function-expr ------> function-expr
         \ --> nodes-function-expr -----/
```

where each of the typed functions may only appear in their respective contexts.

comments.author: danielaparker
comments.body:
> Of what use is syntactic validation by itself? Syntactic validation will say `search(1,2,3,4,5)` is valid. _This is not useful_, so why enable it?

By itself? Well, you detect that there is a function, and you obtain its name, its individual arguments, or report a syntax error. That's useful. 

Semantic validation augments that by verifying that the function name maps to a supported function, the number of arguments matches the expected arity, the return type is valid output, and the types of the arguments are a valid combination of inputs for the function.

In a hand written parser (my understanding is that most JSONPath parsers that implement their own expression language are hand written, certainly all the important ones) semantic validation can be mixed with syntax validation, and allow early detection of unsupported function names, invalid arity, and type errors. But it need not be, it's an implementation choice.

Similar considerations apply to parsing and validating operators.

Especially from a user's point of view, if you have an IDE that can provide hints (e.g. intellisense and/or completion), it doesn't make a difference whether the ABNF is violated or the path just doesn't make sense.

> > Well, you detect that there is a function, and you obtain its name, its individual arguments, or report a syntax error. That's useful.
> 
> But _how_ is it useful?

It produces the tokens to which semantic validation is then applied. That can be later, after an entire parse tree of tokens has been produced, or incrementally in a hand written parser. 

> You saying that it is doesn't make it so

Indeed, but you can also read about it in the Dragon Book. Or the Crafting Compilers book.

A spec writer has some leeway where to put validation, in the ABNF or in the semantic validation. For example, the precedence and associativity rules for operators can be defined in the ABNF, or the spec can simply provide an operator mapping to precedence and associativity rules to be applied in semantic validation.  But generally, it's about the separation of concerns, on the one hand, scanning for tokens, and on the other, applying meaning to them.

Daniel

comments.author: cabo
comments.body:
I think we need to have a slightly sharper terminology to discuss this.

First of all, we have to accept that standards evolve.
Extension points are an approach to make this evolution less painful, but they cannot take the pain away completely.

Note that we don’t have implementations that are intended to interoperate among each other, but we have implementations that operate in an interoperable way on some data.

One objective of the extension point is to achieve backward compatibility, i.e., making sure that evolved systems can interoperably operate on data that was designed at an earlier point of the evolution.
I think we have achieved that.

The other objective of an extension point is forward compatibility: older systems providing some form of successful, interoperable operation when confronted with new data.
Forward compatibility will always be limited: We wouldn’t evolve if we could achieve the new objectives with the older systems as well.

With evolution, there is no way that implementations that are on different levels of evolution can be fully interoperable with all instances.

So what is the limitation here?

What we still could have:

(1) Older systems can successfully detect the presence of an extension they do not support.
So we fully prevent false interoperability.
(2) Extensions have names (the function name), so we can have accurate diagnostics.
(3) In several architectures, will have a way to be added dynamically to existing systems, based on the function name.

These statements require collision-free naming of extensions.
A registry provides the service of collision-free naming.
Other such services can be defined, usually based on hierarchical naming (ASN.1 Object IDs, various forms of URIs, etc.).  Function names are not designed to interface with such naming systems.
RFC 6648 tells us why it is a bad idea to embed a temporary component into what is likely to become a permanent name as deployment of the temporary component spreads.

So what can we improve?

Anyone performing a limited deployment of an extension in order to validate it and complete its detailed definition undergoes a gamble with the name.  
Registering the name early reduces the stakes, but also discloses information (usually, function names should be descriptive).
Registering the name late means there is greater potential for collisions, a risk similar to others that developers already need to manage.

I believe the best contribution we can make is having a good registry policy in place.
Section 3.2 goes a long way, but we probably should have another look.
Obviously, the choice of the designated experts who implement these policies will also influence the success; I believe it is a strength of the IETF registry model that it recognizes that not all decisions can be predetermined in a static ruleset.

Grüße, Carsten

comments.author: glyn
comments.body:
Thanks for those helpful clarifications @danielaparker and @cabo. So, in this PR, I am focussing on consistency of named extensions across implementations. The objective I would like to achieve is that any two implementations should provide consistent behaviour for a function extension with a given name in the sense that:

1. If an implementation does not (yet) support the function extension, any query using the function extension will be rejected with an error.

2. If an implementation supports the function extension, any query using the function extension will behave according to the registered definition of the function extension.

Implementations should also be free to provide a (non-default) mode of operation where unregistered function extensions (perhaps on the way to being registered) are also supported. Users choosing to use such a non-default mode are then running a conscious risk of inconsistent behaviour between implementations.

What should the spec say about such matters? It seems to me that the current spec can be interpreted such that unregistered function extensions can be offered freely to users who could then encounter inconsistent behaviour between implementations. I think the current text of this PR is a step in the direction of making the behaviour more consistent, at least for implementations running in "spec compliant mode".
